meaning: A person may live under a coward's roof and still point to the brave man's house — people admire courage even from the safety of fear.
literal: One stays at the place of a coward and points the hand to the place of the brave one.
usage: Used to describe people who praise bravery loudly while keeping themselves far from danger, or to tease someone whose admiration outstrips their own daring.
igbo: A na-anọ be onye ụjọ atụ aka be dike

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is garbled; it seems to ask whether a woman frightened with a great threat can be expected to lift herself out of it — nobody can hoist themselves out of a danger deliberately made too big for them.
literal: A woman is frightened with a big [,] is it she who will climb herself up?
usage: Said when people expect someone to solve a problem that has been made deliberately too heavy for them.
igbo: A na-atụ nwaanyị ike ukwu ụjọ, ọ bụ ya ga-arigo onwe ya?

meaning: [uncertain] Blocking it does not stop it — what is dammed up or suppressed keeps bursting through.
literal: One blocks Ideyi, it keeps splitting open.
usage: Said when attempts to hold a thing back only make it break out the harder.
igbo: A na-egbochi ideyi, ọ na awa

meaning: [uncertain] One may slaughter the wild beast, but its head is still not as fine as the sheep's — the wild and the foreign never quite match what is bred at home.
literal: One kills ebila; the face is not as good as a sheep's.
usage: Said when a stranger or outsider is being measured against one raised at home, or when something new is compared unfavourably with the familiar.
igbo: A na-egbu ebila ihu anaghị adị atụrụ mma

meaning: The more it is cut back, the more it grows — suppression does not kill what is determined to grow.
literal: One is cutting achara, it is growing.
usage: Said of a person or a matter that thrives the more it is repeatedly stamped on.
igbo: A na-egbu achara ọ na-eto

meaning: [uncertain] With dancing and clapping like this, even the dead will come back to the world — a celebration so great that it draws the ancestors home.
literal: One is dancing and clapping hands and [ikpu]; the dead are returning to the world.
usage: Said at a great celebration, or when an event is so joyful it seems to call the ancestors back.
igbo: A na-egwu egwu na ebisa aka na ikpu, ndị nwụrụ anwụ a na-alọ ụwa

meaning: A worm in the eye must be taken out gently — a delicate and dangerous matter calls for a light hand, not force.
literal: One uses gentleness to scrape the worm out in the eye socket.
usage: Said to advise a soft, patient approach when handling a sensitive person or a risky matter.
igbo: A na-eji nwayọ akọ ụkọ n'iku anya

meaning: [uncertain] The fowl was told it carries filth on its feet, and it answered with its beak — the one accused adds to the charge with his own mouth.
literal: One says that a fowl carries excrement on the legs; it used the mouth to throw it.
usage: Said when someone accused of a fault answers in a way that only makes the case against them stronger.
igbo: A na-ekwu na ọkụkọ bu nshị na okpa, o jiri ọnụ tụrụ ya

meaning: [uncertain] They say the sickness has not yet gone beyond bounds; those who have been struck down still praise the belly — there is always worse to escape, so give thanks for what was spared.
literal: One says that sickness is not enough; those who fell [ibi] are praising the belly.
usage: Offered as consolation to a sick person, or to press someone to be grateful when a bad thing stops short of the worst.
igbo: A na-ekwu na ọrịa ezughị oke, ndị dara ibi na-eto afọ

meaning: [uncertain] A garbled line: a report is said to have reached Father, and the hearer asks whether it reached the mouth of the body too — people want to know how far the news has travelled.
literal: One says that ụkọ ran and met Father; you are asking whether it also ran to the mouth of the body.
usage: Said when a piece of news is being traced to see how far it has spread.
igbo: A na-ekwu n'ụkọ gbara Father, ị na-ajụ ma ọ gbakwara ahụ ọnụ ya

meaning: [uncertain] The line is garbled; it appears to say that one thing is done exactly as the other is done — the same measure is applied to both.
literal: One does ọna, one does ọnammiri.
usage: Said when two people or two cases are being handled with the same measure, or when someone expects to be treated just like another.
igbo: A na-eme ọna a na-eme ọnammiri

meaning: Whatever good is done for a young woman she passes on to the one she loves — a kindness given to one person often ends up serving another.
literal: One does for a girl; she does for the person who is good to her.
usage: Said with a wry tone when a favour done for someone turns out to benefit their favourite instead.
igbo: A na-emere agbọghọ, ya na-emere onye dị ya mma

meaning: You can tell from a child's early days which one will grow up to do great things for his father — what a person will become shows in childhood.
equivalent: The child is father of the man.
literal: One from childhood knows the child who will kill a cow for his father.
usage: Said to point out early signs of character in a child, or to encourage patience with a promising one.
igbo: A na-esi na nwata amara nwa ga-egburu nna ya ehi

meaning: A household's goodness is known first inside the house and then goes out to the public — a family's worth is seen at home before it is seen abroad.
literal: One from the house knows beauty, comes out to the compound.
usage: Said when a family's good name is traced back to how things are kept at home.
igbo: A na-esi n'ụlọ mara mma pụọ ama

meaning: Both hands cannot be pushed into the mouth at once — the appetite must fit the capacity; do not grab at more than you can hold.
equivalent: Don't bite off more than you can chew.
literal: One does not put two hands into the mouth.
usage: A rebuke to greed, or to someone trying to take on everything at once.
igbo: A naghị achịnye aka abụọ na ọnụ

meaning: [uncertain] Whoever walks himself into the muck is the one who has to climb back out of it — you are the one who must get yourself clear of the mess you enter.
literal: If one goes into nshị, one comes climbing out.
usage: Said to someone who has walked into trouble and is looking around for somebody else to pull him out.
igbo: A baa nshị a rịhị

meaning: The kid that keeps out of the butcher's way lives longest — staying clear of danger is what lengthens a life.
literal: If one seeks to kill the kid that hides from the knife, the kid's life grows long.
usage: Used to defend someone who has kept clear of a dangerous venture instead of walking into it.
igbo: A chọwa igbu nwa mkpi na-ezo mma, ndụ nwa mkpi ana-eto ogologo

meaning: [uncertain] When a person insists on opening a matter for talk, something gets said that would have been better left in the dark; the Igbo line here is unclear.
literal: If one seeks the knife of talk, one speaks the thing of the rope at night.
usage: A caution thrown at someone who is determined to start an argument or stir a settled matter.
igbo: A chọwa mma ekwu, e kwuo ihe eriri n'abalị

meaning: When a person is hounded from place to place, he may end up driven into a better place than the one he was chased out of.
literal: When a person has been chased about, one chases him into a good world.
usage: Consolation for someone driven out of his home or refused a place among his own people.
igbo: A chụkata mmadụ, a chụnye ya n'ụwa ọma

meaning: When the sacrifice is made and the vulture, which never misses carrion, fails to appear, it is known that something has gone wrong in the spirit world — the missing sign is itself the sign.
literal: If a sacrifice is offered and the vulture does not see it, it is known that something happened in the land of the spirits.
usage: Reached for when the response one expected to an action simply does not come, and the silence is read as an omen.
igbo: A chụọ aja ahụghi udele amara na ihe mere n'ala ndị mmụọ

meaning: The fact that a bad thing has grown big and long-standing does not make it tradition — size and age do not turn a wrong into a custom.
literal: One does not say that because a bad thing grew a belly, one calls it culture.
usage: A rebuke to those who defend an abuse on the grounds that it has always been done that way.
igbo: A gaghị asị maka na ihe ọjọọ gbara afọ kpọọ ya omenaala

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is obscure; the image is of a digging tool being turned on the user's own eye — the sense seems to be that a thing must not be turned against the one it served.
literal: One does not take it that the hoe dug, and then gouge out the eye.
usage: Said when someone turns a proven tool, skill or habit into his own undoing.
igbo: A gaghị eji na ọkọ kọrọ wee kọpịa anya

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is garbled; it turns on not begrudging what a father arranges and provides for one — a parent's provision is not a thing to be envied or resented.
literal: I will not be jealous that my father married the world for me and finished it off with food.
usage: Said when someone is tempted to resent the way a parent has provided for a relative.
igbo: A gaghị m ekworo na nna m lọọrọ m ụwa nyegbue ya na nri

meaning: When the dancing is over, it comes back to the legs — the doing and its reckoning end with the person who did it.
literal: If the dance is finished, it returns to the leg.
usage: Said when an affair winds up and the person who led it must carry the outcome himself.
igbo: A gbacha egwu, ọ laa n'ukwu

meaning: The miles are counted only after the race has been run — how far it went is reckoned once the effort is over, not before.
literal: If the race is finished, the miles are counted.
usage: Said when someone is drawing conclusions before the work is done.
igbo: A gbachaa ọsọ, agụọ mile

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is unclear; the image is of a crowd agreeing to make a meal of a vulture with the seasoning readied for it — the sense seems to be that a crowd's agreement does not make the thing itself good.
literal: If they gather that the vulture's name be eaten, the ngịga is sprinkled.
usage: A warning against going along with what a crowd has agreed to do.
igbo: A gbakọọ ka aha eri udele, a tọtuo ngịga

meaning: When the chick is seized, its mother has already flown — the one who should have shielded you is gone by the time trouble comes.
literal: If a bird's young is seized, its mother has already flown.
usage: Thrown at someone who counted on backing that never came.
igbo: A gbakwaa nwa nnụnụ, nne ya efelaga

meaning: In a quarrel over land, the one actually holding and working it is the one you must deal with — possession is what the argument comes down to.
literal: When hands are laid on in a land quarrel, it is with the person holding it that one farms yam.
usage: Said in a land dispute to point out who really has the land in hand.
igbo: A gbara aka na-azọ ala, onye ji a na-akọ ji

meaning: To pile up wealth while grudging your own life means that in the end an enemy is the one who eats it.
literal: If one denies life and gathers wealth, an enemy eats it.
usage: A warning to someone working himself to death or hoarding what he never lets himself enjoy.
igbo: A ghara ndụ kpaa akụ, onye iro erie ya

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is unclear; it appears to say that when a matter is told to one person alone, his own world finishes him off — a word given in private is no protection.
literal: If it is told to one person, his world has killed him.
usage: Said when a warning or a charge has been given to a single person and the matter then goes badly.
igbo: A ghaara otu onye, ụwa ya anyịgbuo ya

meaning: An appeal repeated without end wears out, and even the spirits stop hearing it — overuse kills the force of an oath or a plea.
literal: If one keeps declaring ọfọ endlessly, the ears of the spirits are blocked.
usage: Thrown at someone who swears oaths or repeats a plea too often, as a warning that he is wearing his own appeal thin.
igbo: A gọwa ọfọ ebighi ebi, nti echie ndi mmụọ

meaning: When a thing has been settled once and for all, you do not come back to patch it in little bits — half-measures are no cure, and a finished matter should be left finished.
literal: When a mad person has been treated all over, one does not treat him in little bits.
usage: Used to close a matter that somebody keeps reopening, or to insist that a job be done completely rather than in dribs.
igbo: A gwọchagodi onye ara, anaghị agwọta ya ntakwu

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is unclear; it seems to say that a person left alone is undone by his own world — abandoned to himself, he is destroyed by his own circumstances.
literal: If one person was left alone, his world has killed him.
usage: Said of someone who has been left to fend for himself and is now in trouble.
igbo: A haara otu onye, ụwa ya anyịgbuo ya

meaning: [uncertain] The line is garbled and incomplete, and its sense cannot be recovered; it appears to concern strength that is let go or an advantage divided by force.
literal: If strength is let go, the one who gave was seen; let the head of ọkpọ be shared out.
usage: An obscure local line, used only where the full proverb is known, of effort or advantage thrown away.
igbo: A hapụ ike nyụrụ ahụrụ ekee isi ọkpọ

meaning: A capable man is known the moment you set eyes on him — his worth shows in his very bearing.
literal: If one sees a strong man, one sees his long nose.
usage: Said in praise or recognition of someone whose ability is plain at first sight.
igbo: A hụ dimkpa, ahụ ogologo imi ya

meaning: When something better than what you already have comes into view, you part with everything you own to get it — the bigger prize is worth selling off the store.
literal: If one sees a thing more than the farm, one sells the granary.
usage: Said when someone stakes everything on a promising new opening.
igbo: A hụ ihe ka ubi e ree ọba

meaning: [uncertain] The line is corrupt and overlong; on its face it speaks of there being no bridewealth for the first daughter while all the daughters are pregnant and bearing sons, but the point cannot be recovered with confidence.
literal: The money to marry off the first daughter was not seen; all the daughters are pregnant, and one keeps giving birth to male, male.
usage: An obscure saying about bridewealth and childbearing in a family, reached for only where it is locally known.
igbo: A hụghị ego lụnye ọkpara nwaanyị ụmụ nwaanyị niile di ime a na-mụ nwoke nwoke

meaning: What was done where nobody could see it must be done again in the open — a deed kept in the dark is bound to come into the light.
literal: One did not see how it was done; let it be done so that one saw.
usage: Said when demanding that a thing be redone openly, or when hinting that a secret act will be exposed.
igbo: A hụghị ka e mere, e mee ka a hụrụ

meaning: [uncertain] The line does not parse cleanly; it appears to turn on inquiry and its reward — that asking, rather than refusing to ask, is what keeps a person from sickness and death.
literal: One did not refuse the asking, and eating brings about not being sick and not dying.
usage: An obscure line about inquiry and health, used where the proverb is locally known.
igbo: A jụghị ajụ eri na-ebute arịaghị arịa anwụ

meaning: [uncertain] Garbled and cut short; something about not being refused while being called out in the course of trading, but the sense is not recoverable.
literal: I was not refused, but I was called, as I was selling and selling.
usage: A market saying, used only where the proverb is known in full.
igbo: A jụghị m ma akpọwara m akpọwa ka m na-ere ere

meaning: A thing done openly and in its right season is enjoyed in one's own lifetime — act while you can, and you will eat the fruit yourself.
literal: If one tells or plants it in the sun, one eats in life.
usage: Said to press someone to act now, openly and in good time, instead of putting things off.
igbo: A kọọ n'anwu, e rie na ndụ

meaning: [uncertain] A truncated fragment — 'if it has been told or planted, it is ...' — with no recoverable sense.
literal: If it has been told or planted, it has been ... (the rest is garbled).
usage: A fragment recorded as it stands; a speaker would have to know the full line to use it.
igbo: A kọruo e geruo

meaning: You rest in the comfort your own hands have prepared — the bed you make is the one you lie in.
equivalent: As you make your bed, so you must lie in it.
literal: If one makes the bedding, one sleeps on the mat.
usage: Said to remind someone that the situation he lies down in was arranged by his own hands.
igbo: A kpaa akpaa a rahụọ n'ute

meaning: [uncertain] Obscure and possibly mistyped; on the surface it questions whether the medicine itself refuses, and likely warns against scorning or withholding a remedy.
literal: Do not administer the medicine; is it that it refuses?
usage: A local saying about medicine, used where the proverb is known.
igbo: A kụla ọgwụ, ọ bụ ma ajụ?

meaning: [uncertain] Truncated; the ekwe drum is sounded and something follows about the village, but the line breaks off before its point.
literal: If the ekwe is sounded, the ... 'ama agbaa' (the line breaks off).
usage: A fragment of a drum-announcement proverb, used only where the full form is known.
igbo: A kụọ ekwe ama agbaa

meaning: [uncertain] Offering the sacrifice is what brings the quarrel into the open — the very act of settling a matter stirs up the fight.
literal: If one offers sacrifice, one sees a fight.
usage: Said when a peace-making gesture ends up opening a fresh quarrel.
igbo: A kwaa aja a hụ ọgụ

meaning: [uncertain] Even a strong man can be made to feel fear once his chest is patted and he is soothed — comfort softens the fierce.
literal: If a strong man's chest is patted, fear is put into him.
usage: Used to warn that gentleness or flattery can take the edge off a fierce person.
igbo: A kwakata dike aka n'obi, a kwanye ya ụjọ

meaning: [uncertain] The line is corrupt; it seems to say the work is finished and yet something still has to be pulled out — a completed task can leave a hidden part behind.
literal: If one stands and finishes the yam, one does not come back to pull out its tail.
usage: Said when a job looks done but something is still left sticking out.
igbo: A kwụrụ ọtọ gwujie ji, ehulọta gwuputa ọdụ ya

meaning: [uncertain] A young bride is brought in and the old woman is driven out — the new displaces the old.
literal: If a girl is married in, the old one is chased away.
usage: Said when something new pushes aside what came before it.
igbo: A lụta agbọghọ, a chụpụ agadị

meaning: [uncertain] Knowing the water that hides itself away and knowing the water that spreads in the open go together — a discerning person sees both.
literal: If one knows the water that hid in secret, one knows the one that spread out.
usage: Used in praise of someone who notices what others overlook, hidden or plain.
igbo: A ma mmiri zoro ozo, mara nke tasara atasa

meaning: [uncertain] The fire that warmed your hands is not thrown away but kept on the wall rack — do not cast off what has served you, for you may need it again.
literal: If fire is kindled for licking the hand, it will be hung up on the wall.
usage: Said of someone who remembers a past kindness and keeps the giver close.
igbo: A na-achi ọkụ aracha aka, a ga-ekonye ya n'uko

meaning: [uncertain] Advice is aimed at the child whose mother is alive; the motherless child hears the same words with no one standing behind him.
literal: One advises the child who has a mother; the one without a mother is listening.
usage: Said to show how a mother's presence backs up the training her child receives.
igbo: A na-adụ nwa nwere nne ọdụ nke na enweghi nne na-egere

meaning: [uncertain] The words are corrupt; they appear to say that warning a thief who already carries the mark of his guilt only makes him bolder.
literal: One warns the thief who has a tail; he takes heart and thumps his back.
usage: Said when a warning given to a guilty person only makes him more brazen.
igbo: A na-adụ onye oshi ji ọdụ, ya were obi na-apịa mbazụ

meaning: People go out to the gathering for the company of other people, not for a sight everyone already has at home — the moon shines in every compound, so it is the crowd that draws you.
literal: One goes to the moon dance so as to see people, not so as to see the moon, because the moon shines in every person's compound.
usage: Said to explain that people seek one another out, not spectacle.
igbo: A na-aga egwu ọnwa ka ahụ mmadụ ọ bụghị ka ahụ ọnwa, maka ọnwa na-eti n'ụlọ onye ọbụla

meaning: Travel broadens the mind — you go to other lands to learn something, not to fill your belly.
equivalent: Travel broadens the mind
literal: One goes to other lands so as to learn something, not so as to fill the belly.
usage: Said to urge that a journey be made for knowledge and not merely for food or gain.
igbo: A na-aga mba ka amụta ihe ọ bụghị ka e rijue afọ

meaning: [uncertain] The line is corrupt; it appears to say that every consultation comes back with death, death.
literal: Divination is done over it, and it keeps falling as death, death.
usage: Said where every inquiry or sign points the same grim way.
igbo: A na-agba afa na agụọ, ọ na-ada ọnwụ ọnwụ

meaning: You do not put pepper into eyes that are already sore — do not rub in what someone is already suffering.
literal: One is speaking to the yellow eyes; one does not put pepper into them.
usage: Said to stop someone from pressing a person who is already in pain.
igbo: A na-agwa odo anya anaghị etinye ya ose

meaning: [uncertain] The words are corrupt; the sense may be that the treatment only makes the sickness swell.
literal: It is being treated; it vomits and the belly keeps swelling.
usage: Said when a remedy makes worse the very trouble it was meant to cure.
igbo: A na-agwọ ya ibi ya na-eto afọ

meaning: [uncertain] Another person's effort can only be guessed at — he merely looks as though he is working.
literal: One guesses at Otule; he looks as if he is at work.
usage: Said of someone whose busy appearance is no proof that he is really working.
igbo: A na-ama atụ otule, ọ dịka ọ nọ n'oru

meaning: How high the water will rise can be told from the rain that fell — a thing is judged by what produced it.
literal: One knows the level of the water by its rainfall.
usage: Said when explaining that an outcome can be read from its cause.
igbo: A na-ama ọkwa mmiri maka ozuzo ya

meaning: You do not pile more trouble onto someone who is already busy chasing something of their own.
literal: One does not seek the thing that troubles a person who is seeking something.
usage: Used to check someone who keeps adding demands to a person already struggling with their own errand.
igbo: A naghị achọ ihe na-akpa onye na-achọ ihe

meaning: A person of worth is not found hidden among the common crowd; you do not go looking for a prince in a throng of ordinary people.
literal: One does not seek the child of a king in the crowd of the people.
usage: Said of someone whose quality shows wherever they stand, or to turn a search away from the wrong crowd.
igbo: A naghị achọ nwa eze achọ n'ọgbọ ọha

meaning: [uncertain] A king's child is not to be laid hands on — some people must be handled with care and respect.
literal: One does not lay a hand on the child of a king.
usage: A caution against taking liberties with a person who must be treated with respect.
igbo: A naghi agba aka ahụ nwata eze

meaning: [uncertain] A kola nut set apart for ritual is not to be handled carelessly — sacred things are not for casual hands.
literal: One does not lay a hand on the arị kola nut.
usage: A warning to keep careless hands off what is sacred or set apart.
igbo: A naghị agba aka arị ọjị

meaning: See to the greatest need first; do not scratch the small itch and leave the big one alone.
literal: One does not scratch the itch of the hand and leave the head.
usage: A rebuke to someone who settles a small matter and leaves the pressing one untouched.
igbo: A naghi agba ụria aka hapụ isi aka

meaning: [uncertain] What the body must bring out cannot be argued away — hidden things surface in the end.
literal: One does not plead on behalf of the excrement inside the belly.
usage: Said of a matter that cannot be hidden or talked away and must sooner or later come out.
igbo: A naghị agbara nshị nọ n'afọ asụ

meaning: You do not tell an expert how his own trade is done; he knows it better than you.
equivalent: Don't teach your grandmother to suck eggs.
literal: One does not tell the dibia that there is work in the medicine.
usage: Used when someone explains to a specialist what the specialist already knows.
igbo: A naghị agwa diochi na ọrụ di na ngwọ

meaning: You do not announce to the person in charge what is plain to everyone; whoever is responsible already knows it.
literal: One does not tell the head one that there is no salt in the soup.
usage: A mild rebuke to someone who points out the obvious to the person responsible for it.
igbo: A naghị agwa onye isi na nnu adịghị n’ofe

meaning: [uncertain] There is no point carrying news to someone who was bound to hear it anyway.
literal: One does not tell the long-eared one that the market has burnt down.
usage: Said when someone rushes to inform a person who would have heard the news regardless.
igbo: A naghi agwa oshi ntị na ahịa esula

meaning: [uncertain] Do not abandon a good and settled place for one that promises trouble.
literal: One does not leave the place where ọzọ is being observed and go to the place where agwụ is being worked.
usage: A warning against giving up a good situation for one that looks like trouble.
igbo: A naghi ahapụ ebe ana-echi ọzọ jebe ebe a na arụ agwụ

meaning: [uncertain] Do not throw away the valuable thing and pick up the worthless one.
literal: One does not abandon isi aka and take up agba ụrịọm.
usage: A rebuke to someone who trades a good thing for a poor one.
igbo: A naghị ahapụ isiaka were agba ụrịọm

meaning: [uncertain] Do not clear everything away and then expect someone else to gather from what is left.
literal: One does not clear the whole road and say, learn firewood.
usage: Said to someone who uses everything up and then expects others to make do with nothing.
igbo: A naghị ahụcha ụzọ sị mụta okụ

meaning: Do not refuse food that has been set aside and covered for you; a portion prepared in advance is not to be turned down.
literal: One does not refuse food that has been covered over and over.
usage: Said to urge someone to accept a gift that has already been prepared for them.
igbo: A naghị ajụ nri ekpusiri ekpusi

meaning: Do not refuse a dish because it comes covered; accept what is set before you before judging it.
literal: One does not refuse a plate along with its cover.
usage: Said to encourage someone to accept what is offered rather than turning it down sight unseen.
igbo: A naghị ajụ efere na nkwuchi

meaning: Do not judge a wanderer by where they spent the night; what matters more is that they came home.
literal: One does not refuse okokporo because of where it slept at night; the more important thing is whether it came back home.
usage: A consolation offered when someone who strayed has found their way back.
igbo: A naghị ajụ okokporo ebe ọ rahụrụ ụra na abalị, ihe ka mkpa bụ ma ọ lọtarakwara

meaning: [uncertain] The saying points to impossibility: you cannot make water foam fire by working it in your mouth; you cannot force something to yield what it does not have.
literal: One does not cut water in the mouth [and] it foams fire.
usage: Used to dismiss a demand or scheme that tries to make something produce what it cannot produce.
igbo: A naghị akpụ mmiri n'ọnụ afụ okụ

meaning: [uncertain] The proverb warns against washing up only to immediately do a messy task, or against wasted preparation.
literal: One does not wash hands [and then] pound chicken [and] palm kernel.
usage: Said when someone cleans up only to get dirty again right away.
igbo: A naghị akwọ aka etiri ọkụkọ akị

meaning: You do not learn a craft with the left hand; serious work must be done with your full, stronger effort.
literal: One does not learn the left hand in a craft.
usage: Used to urge someone not to approach a task half-heartedly.
igbo: A naghị amụ aka ekpe na nka

meaning: You do not stand in the front line of battle cracking palm kernels; do not occupy yourself with trifles when danger is at hand.
equivalent: Fiddling while Rome burns
literal: One does not stay in front of a fight cracking palm kernels.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who is distracted by small matters in a serious situation.
igbo: A naghị anọ n'ihu ọgụ apị akụ

meaning: You cannot watch a masquerade from one fixed spot; you must move with it. Do not expect to see everything from a single position.
literal: One does not stay in one place to watch a masquerade.
usage: Said to someone who insists on one fixed approach when flexibility is needed.
igbo: A naghị anọ ofu ebe ekiri mmanwụ

meaning: When you hear the words of spirits, you do not open your mouth wide; you keep silent and listen.
literal: One does not hear the head of the spirits and open the mouth wide.
usage: Used to reprove someone who talks when they should be listening to important or sacred matters.
igbo: A naghị anụ isi ndi mmụọ ghewe ọnụ oghe

meaning: [uncertain] You cannot claim a woman is finished or helpless; you do not know where she draws her strength from.
literal: One does not say a woman has finished closing her legs; one does not know where she breathes from.
usage: Said as a warning not to underestimate a woman's hidden resources or resilience.
igbo: A naghị asi agadị nwaanyị mechikụlọta ụkwụ, a maghị ebe o si eku ume

meaning: You do not send an elder out into the hot sun to do work; elders are not given hardship errands.
literal: One does not say an elder should come out into the sun.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who sends an elder on a strenuous errand or exposes them to hardship.
igbo: A naghị asị okenye pụta n'anwụ

meaning: [uncertain] You cannot chew a bone in secret; the noise will give you away, so hidden things come to light.
literal: One does not chew bone [or] jawbone in secret.
usage: Said when someone tries to keep a matter hidden but it is bound to be discovered.
igbo: A naghị ata okpụkpụ nshịkọ na nzuzo

meaning: You should not decide a case after hearing only one side; hear both sides before judging.
equivalent: One story is good till another is told
literal: One does not judge a case with one voice.
usage: Used to caution someone who is ready to condemn another after hearing only one account.
igbo: A naghị ebi ikpe n'otu olu

meaning: You do not bring something to a place where it already abounds; do not offer what is already plentiful there.
equivalent: Don't carry coals to Newcastle
literal: One does not carry firewood to the ụkpaka tree.
usage: Said when someone brings supplies or advice to people who already have plenty of it.
igbo: A naghi ebute ụkwa n'osisi ụkpaka

meaning: You do not encourage a child to learn to make fire and then pour water on it; do not build up an effort only to quench it.
literal: One does not allow a child to learn fire, [and then] sprinkle water on it.
usage: Said when someone first encourages a beginner and then immediately discourages or undoes the lesson.
igbo: A naghi edinye nwata mụta ọkụ, hakwasị ya mmiri

meaning: You do not send a child to fetch salt and then pour water on it; do not undermine the errand you entrusted to someone.
literal: One does not allow a child [to go on] an errand for salt, [and then] sprinkle water on it.
usage: Said to someone who spoils or cancels the very task they entrusted to another.
igbo: A naghi edinye nwata ozi nnụ, hakwasị ya mmiri

meaning: You do not lead a goat into the barn; do not entrust something to someone who will destroy it.
equivalent: Don't set a fox to guard the henhouse
literal: One does not lead a goat to the barn.
usage: Used to warn against putting a destructive person in charge of what they will ruin.
igbo: A naghi edu ewu eje n'ọba

meaning: [uncertain] You do not use the night to look for what needs daylight, or to expect to see clearly in darkness.
literal: One does not use the night to seek eyes.
usage: Said when someone tries to do at night what should be done in daylight, or expects results at the wrong time.
igbo: A naghị eji abalị arọ anya

meaning: Water gathered into one place foams: small things brought together gain a force they never had apart.
literal: If water is gathered together at one mouth, it foams.
usage: Said to draw scattered people or small contributions into a common effort, or in praise of what a group achieves together.
igbo: A nyụkọọ mamịrị ọnụ, ọ gba ụfụfụ

meaning: [uncertain] The line is corrupt as it stands; the sense appears to be that a foul thing poured out and left unsealed goes on stinking — a messy matter left open keeps doing damage.
literal: If excrement is poured out and it is not closed at the mouth, it becomes otoro.
usage: Used to urge someone to contain a shameful or messy matter rather than leave it open to fester.
igbo: A nyụọ nshị akapịghị ọnụ, ọ bụrụ otoro

meaning: Work done in the hard dry season is what you eat in the season of living — labour now, enjoy later.
literal: If one works in the sun (dry season), one eats in life.
usage: Said to push someone through lean, unglamorous work, or in praise of foresight.
igbo: A rụọ n'anwụ, e rie na ndụ

meaning: Tell a thief to catch a fowl and he says he will eat it first — a person's real nature shows the moment you put the chance in his hand.
literal: If one says to a thief, catch a fowl, he says that he will first eat it.
usage: A warning against handing anything to someone whose appetite is known, or a wry comment when a bad habit shows at once.
igbo: A sị onye ohi nwude ọkụkọ ọ si na ọ ga-atagbu ya

meaning: A child has no yardstick of his own for goodness: told to greet a good person, he calls her his mother's friend — children see the world through their parents' ties.
literal: If one tells a child to greet a good person, he greets her as his mother's friend.
usage: Said lightly when a child's loyalties and judgements simply mirror the family's own circle.
igbo: A sị nwata kpọọ onye ọma, ọ kpọọ enyi nne ya

meaning: [uncertain] Where the king is too great to be addressed face to face, one speaks to him with a basket held up before one — the powerful are approached with covering and indirection.
literal: If the king is greatly revered/fearsome, one covers with a basket and speaks to him.
usage: Used when advising someone to show deference, or to reach a great person by an indirect and respectful route.
igbo: A sọgide eze, ekpuru nkata gwa ya okwu

meaning: [uncertain] Tapping the ụkwa is tapping the akị as well — the sense appears to be that things of one kind are handled together and one act draws its twin along with it.
literal: One taps the ụkwa, one taps the akị.
usage: Said when one thing unavoidably drags its companion along with it.
igbo: A tatụ ụkwa a tatụ akị

meaning: Throw away the thing by which beauty is judged and beauty itself goes bad — worth can only be seen through the standard that shows it.
literal: If one throws away the thing with which beauty is known, beauty goes bad.
usage: A caution against despising the elders, tools or standards by which excellence is recognised.
igbo: A tụfuo ihe e ji ama mma, mma arụọ

meaning: [uncertain] The line is corrupt as it stands; the sense seems to be that a small part thrown away today will be searched for on the day it is needed.
literal: If the nkịrịnka of the basket is thrown away, the day sacrifice is made, it will be looked for.
usage: A warning not to discard a small thing that will be wanted on the day of need.
igbo: A tụfuo nkịrịnka nkata, ubọchị a ga achụ aja ruo, a chọwa ya

meaning: When a proverb is aimed, the face of the person it fits darkens — the one it is meant for feels the pinch.
literal: If a proverb is told (with) the nkịrịnka of the basket, the face of the one who tasted the body spoils.
usage: Said when a pointed saying lands, as a gentle way of noting whose case the words describe.
igbo: A tụọ ilu nkịrịnka nkata, ihu agbajọọ onye tara ahụ

meaning: Told to one who knows, a word lands and he understands; told to a fool, he flings his head into the bush and nothing enters.
literal: If it is told to the knowing one, he knows; if it is told to the fool, he throws his head into the bush.
usage: Said when advice is wasted on someone who will not hear it, or in praise of a person who takes correction quickly.
igbo: A tụọrọ ọ mara ọ mara, a tụọrọ ofeke o fenye isi n'ọhịa

meaning: [uncertain] The line is partly garbled; the sense appears to be that when you toss something to a puppy you should show it clearly, so it does not take the throw for a blow.
literal: One throws igwi to a puppy, one shows it to it, so that it does not think that you threw mbọ at it.
usage: Said of making your intention plain to the young or the weak, so a kindness is not mistaken for an attack.
igbo: A tụpụ nwa nkịta igwi, egosi ya, ka ọ ghara iche na ị tụrụ ya mbọ

meaning: A proverb is told so that it may turn even the fool around — the roundabout word is aimed at changing someone.
literal: A proverb is told that it may turn the fool around.
usage: Said to explain why a speaker wrapped a correction in a proverb instead of saying it straight out.
igbo: A tụrụ ilu ka ọ gba ofeke gharịị

meaning: When the beans are shelled the husks go on the dunghill — what has given up its use is thrown away.
literal: If beans are cracked out of the pod, the husk is thrown into the dunghill.
usage: A sober or cutting remark when someone is set aside once he is no longer of use.
igbo: A tụwa agwa ahụrụ a baa nshị

meaning: When a life is saved, death is only set aside — rescue buys time, it does not cancel the debt.
literal: If a life is saved, death is kept aside.
usage: Said after a narrow escape, as consolation and sober reminder, or to urge that saving a life is what matters most.
igbo: A zọta ndu, edebere ọnwụ

meaning: A blow aimed at an unshakeable person lands only on their shell — some people cannot be hurt by the attacks meant for them.
literal: The snake struck the tortoise, it struck the shell.
usage: Said when someone's attack glances off a well-protected person, or to reassure someone whose enemies have failed to touch them.
igbo: Agwọ tụrụ mbe, tụrụ okpokoro

meaning: [uncertain] Possibly: a good name counts for nothing in the noise of a rowdy crowd; the recorded line is unclear and the sense cannot be fixed with confidence.
literal: My name does not fare well in the crowd's din.
usage: Offered as a lament that a person's standing goes unheard and unrecognised where everyone is shouting at once.
igbo: Aha m anaghị adị mma na mkporohihi

meaning: Real quality recommends itself; a thing that is genuinely good needs no one to advertise it.
equivalent: Good wine needs no bush.
literal: A market that is good sells itself.
usage: Said in praise of genuine quality, or to tell someone anxious about promotion that good work speaks for itself.
igbo: Ahịa dị mma na-ere onwe

meaning: Trade confined to one's own kind brings no gain — a trader who sells only among his own people makes no profit.
literal: The market of tortoises dealing with tortoises, profit does not exist in it.
usage: Used to urge someone to widen his dealings beyond his own circle instead of trading only with his kinsmen.
igbo: Ahịa mbe na mbe na-azụ uru anaghị adị na ya

meaning: Real quality recommends itself; a thing that is genuinely good needs no one to advertise it.
equivalent: Good wine needs no bush.
literal: A good market sells itself.
usage: Said in praise of genuine quality, or to tell someone anxious about promotion that good work speaks for itself.
igbo: Ahịa ọma na-ere onwe ya

meaning: What a buyer gets out of a market depends on how sharp his own eyes are — the buyer must judge for himself.
literal: The market of the one who buys is as good as his eyes.
usage: Said to put the responsibility on a buyer or a chooser: look carefully, because no one else will look for you.
igbo: Ahịa onye na-azụ ka ọma anya ya

meaning: The noise is heard once the market has closed — the reckoning and the talk come only after the deed is done.
literal: When the market is finished, one hears its sound.
usage: Said to someone who thinks an affair is neatly finished, as a reminder that the aftermath will still be heard.
igbo: Ahịa zụchaa a nụ ụda ya

meaning: [uncertain] Judging the taste of a soup by the look of its surface — appearances taken for the truth of a thing; the recorded line is unclear.
literal: See the face of the soup, speak out the taste.
usage: Used as a caution to someone who pronounces on a matter from its outward look alone.
igbo: Ahụ ihu ofe, asụta ụtara

meaning: [uncertain] The recorded line is corrupt; it seems to speak of something seen up high that drove flies about, but no reliable sense can be given.
literal: What was seen on top drove flies around.
usage: Cannot be used with confidence; the proverb as recorded is not intelligible enough to place in speech.
igbo: Ahụrụ anyụrụ n'elu gbara ijiji gharị

meaning: [uncertain] The line is unclear; if it means that one gave the in-law no answer and simply sat down, the point is that silence is the best reply to provocation.
literal: Ahushie the in-law, one did not answer it and took a seat.
usage: Offered, cautiously, where someone is advised to say nothing back and simply take his seat.
igbo: Ahụshie ọgọ a nazịghị asị ya were oche

meaning: Hardship makes people see with bad eyes — want and misery breed envy and suspicion.
literal: A bad condition brought looking with bad eyes.
usage: Said to excuse or explain a person's envy, laying the blame on the hard circumstances rather than on the person.
igbo: Ajọ ọnọdụ butere ile ajọ anya

meaning: A wicked child will threaten even the mother who bore him — ingratitude turns on its own source.
literal: A bad child said he would enter his mother's belly.
usage: Said in rebuke of an ingrate who bites the hand that raised him.
igbo: Ajọ nwa siri owere baa nne ya afọ

meaning: Work that soils the hands puts rich food in the mouth — hard, dirty labour is what earns a good living.
literal: A sandy hand brings about an oily mouth.
usage: Said to encourage someone in hard or dirty work, or to shame those who want the reward without the labour.
igbo: Aka aja aja na-ebute ọnụ mmanụ mmanụ

meaning: One hand cannot hide the moon — some things are too big and too bright to be concealed.
literal: A hand covers the moon.
usage: Said to someone trying to keep an obvious wrongdoing quiet, as a warning that it will be seen.
igbo: Aka ekpuchi ọnwa

meaning: If a hand can snap iron, then wood has every reason to tremble — the fate of the stronger is a warning to the weaker.
literal: The hand has broken iron; let wood fear.
usage: Said as a warning to a lesser opponent after the stronger one has been brought down.
igbo: Aka gbajie igwe ụjọ atụọ osisi

meaning: [uncertain] The one who knows what he has done keeps silent, shutting off every opening.
literal: Abụzụ who knows what it did, shut its anus, shut its mouth.
usage: Said of someone who knows the truth but refuses to speak.
igbo: Abụzụ maara ihe o mere gbachie ụpụ gbachie isi ọnụ

meaning: When looking for where to begin, start from the nearest and most basic point.
literal: Searching for where one will start hand, start at the knee.
usage: Used to urge someone to begin with what is close at hand instead of waiting for ideal conditions.
igbo: Achọgide ebe a ga ebido aka, ebido n'ikpere

meaning: Hunger will not let a person rest; need drives one to keep moving.
literal: The stomach did not allow the leg to rest.
usage: Said to explain why someone cannot afford to sit idle.
igbo: Afọ ekweghi ụkwụ zuo ike

meaning: [uncertain] A healthy appetite and food ready at hand are a fortunate match.
literal: A good stomach with a tuber on the ground.
usage: Said when desire and opportunity come together.
igbo: Afọ ọma ya na akpụ n'ala

meaning: A community does not feel the absence of one person; the market continues without them.
literal: Umuduru's stomach does not know that one person did not come to market.
usage: Said when someone overestimates their importance to a group.
igbo: Afọ Umuduru amaghị na ofu onye abiaghị ahịa

meaning: Experience makes an elder competent in the things she knows.
literal: An old woman does not lack skill in the dance she knows how to dance.
usage: Said in praise of an elder's expertise or to remind others that experience counts.
igbo: Agadi nwaanyị anaghị aka nka n'egwu ọ ma agba

meaning: A second failure makes one stop and examine the burden one is carrying.
literal: When an old woman falls down twice, she counts what she carries on her head.
usage: Said to urge someone to learn from repeated mistakes.
igbo: Agadi nwaanyị daa ada ugboro abụọ, ọ gụọ ihe o bu n'ísi ọnụ

meaning: Do not underestimate someone because they seem weak or harmless.
equivalent: Don't judge a book by its cover.
literal: An old woman was entrusted with a child; she said it had no teeth; then it bit her badly.
usage: Said when someone dismisses another as incapable and is proved wrong.
igbo: Agadi nwaanyị e kunyere nwa, ọ sị ya enwezighi eze, a sọ ya tagbuo ya atagbu

meaning: [uncertain] Each side is scheming against the other, each planning to consume or defeat the other.
literal: An old woman is thinking how she will eat inine; the inine is thinking how it will wash the woman's stomach.
usage: Said when two parties are secretly plotting against each other.
igbo: Agadi nwaanyị na-eche ka ọ ga-esi ri inine, inine a na-eche ka ọga-esi saa nwaanyị afọ

meaning: When someone has support, they boast of their family's ability.
literal: An elder who has someone caring for her says that her lineage does not lack skill.
usage: Said of a person who becomes boastful once they have backing.
igbo: Agadi nwere onye na-elekọta ya, sị na agbụrụ ya anaghị aka nka

meaning: [uncertain] I will not step into a place or role prepared for another.
literal: I will not enter the oba that was made for ede.
usage: Said when refusing to take on another person's place or responsibility.
igbo: Agaghị m aba n'ọba e kere ede

meaning: Without preparation, even strength cannot carry one through.
literal: If the road is not cleared, even with wrestling it does not pass.
usage: Said to urge clearing the way before relying on force.
igbo: Agbaghị ụzọ owerre mgba ọnaghị eshi

meaning: [uncertain] A powerful spirit that runs on sand eats an inferior goat; perhaps power does not always match the offering, or one accepts what is unworthy.
literal: Agbara that runs on sand, eating a bad goat.
usage: Said of someone whose conduct belies their claimed stature.
igbo: Agbara na-agba ọsọ aja, na-eri ewu ọjọọ

meaning: [uncertain] The text is garbled; its sense cannot be recovered with confidence.
literal: Agbarụọ ngele was scooped and drunk.
usage: Cannot be determined from the surviving text.
igbo: Agbarụọ ngele e kuru ṅụọ

meaning: Your neighbor is your brother or sister; neighbors are family.
literal: A person's neighbor is his sibling.
usage: Said to encourage good neighborliness and mutual care.
igbo: Agbataobi onye bụ nwanne ya

meaning: [uncertain] Do not come with a careless eye to look at something that is itself all eyes: you cannot out-watch the watchful, and the attempt only exposes you.
literal: One does not use a roving eye to go to the atanị's, because atanị is eyes eyes.
usage: A warning to someone who believes he can quietly get the better of a far sharper, more vigilant person.
igbo: A naghị eji anya nchakasị aga na nke atanị, maka atanị bụ anya anya

meaning: What is made for the ear must not be used on the eye — a case must be met with the remedy that suits it, not with a rougher one borrowed from elsewhere.
literal: One does not use the thing that is pierced into the ear to pierce into the eye.
usage: Said to fault someone who applies a crude or unsuitable measure to a delicate matter.
igbo: A naghị eji ihe ana-agba na ntị agba n'anya

meaning: Shame should not make a person swallow an attempt — being embarrassed is no reason to give up what one meant to do.
literal: One does not use shame to swallow a trial.
usage: Used to push someone who is hanging back out of embarrassment to go ahead and try.
igbo: A naghị eji ihere elo anwa

meaning: You do not wait until the dance is finished and then start clapping — support and praise must come while they still count, not after the matter is closed.
literal: One does not finish the dance and then clap hands on the chest.
usage: A rebuke to those who show their support or gratitude only after the need has passed.
igbo: A naghị enwecha nkwa, na-akwa aka n'ume

meaning: You do not hand a dog a bone and then tell it to guard it — never put a thing in the keeping of the one who will consume it.
equivalent: Don't set a fox to guard the henhouse.
literal: One does not give a dog a bone and tell it to keep watch over it.
usage: Said when a valuable thing is entrusted to the very person most likely to devour it.
igbo: A naghị enye nkịta ọkpụkpọ sị ya chebe

meaning: You do not sell a short-legged fowl close to home — a flaw everyone can see cannot be passed off on those who already know it.
literal: One does not sell a short-legged chicken nearby.
usage: Said of a person trying to palm off something defective on neighbours who can see the defect plainly.
igbo: A naghị ere ọkụkọ ụkwụ mkpirisi na nso

meaning: You do not beat a child over the thing that has already carried off his cloth — do not add punishment to a misfortune the person has already suffered.
literal: One does not beat a child the thing that took his cloth.
usage: A consolation and a gentle rebuke, said when someone is being scolded for a loss he could not help.
igbo: A naghị eti nwata ihe nara ya akwa

meaning: [uncertain] A child is not to be beaten for the day he spilled the palm oil any more than for the day he knocked over the ogiri pot — the mishaps are of one kind, and neither makes him a culprit.
literal: One does not beat a child the day he spilled oil, or the day he spilled the ogiri pot.
usage: Used to stop someone from punishing one accident far more harshly than another just as small.
igbo: A naghị eti nwata ihe ụbọchị ọ wụfuru mmanụ ka ma ọ bụ ụbọchị ọ wụfuru ogiri akwụ

meaning: [uncertain] Do not strike at a masquerade while the crowd is clapping for it.
literal: One does not beat the masquerade that hands are being clapped for.
usage: A warning not to take on a figure the community is at that very moment celebrating.
igbo: A naghị m eti mmọnwụ a na-akwa aka

meaning: [uncertain] Take the fish-work from one person and you have already taken it from his neighbour — a wrong done to one is felt by all.
literal: One takes one person's work of fish, one has taken his fellow's.
usage: Said to show that robbing or cheating one person is an injury to the whole group.
igbo: A nara ofu onye oru azụ, a narago ibe ya

meaning: [uncertain] Nobody takes up a wrestling bout in order to throw his money away — do not enter a contest whose only stake is your own loss.
literal: One does not answer a wrestling bout so that I drop money.
usage: Said of someone entering an undertaking that can only cost him what he puts in.
igbo: A nazịghị m agba ka m data ego

meaning: [uncertain] People will sit and talk of spirits and spirits while a living person is right there in front of them — the far-off wonder is preferred to the person at hand.
literal: A person is being present, and people are talking spirits spirits.
usage: Used when people chase marvels and overlook the person or the fact standing right before them.
igbo: A nọdị mmadụ mmadụ a na-ekwu mmụọ mmụọ

meaning: [uncertain] A truncated line — 'one keeps on staying about' — which appears to be about holding one's ground or persisting, but the text is too short to fix its sense.
literal: One continues to stay about.
usage: Unclear; as recorded the line is too short to place in a conversation.
igbo: A nọgide anọgharịa

meaning: [uncertain] Whoever plants himself up high is seen by all, and the flies swarm him — prominence draws attack.
literal: One stays on top and is seen; a swarm of flies will gather.
usage: Said to someone who draws attention to himself and then complains of being picked at.
igbo: A nọrọ n'elu nyụọ ahụrụ, ọgba ijiji gharịị

meaning: [uncertain] The line is garbled; it appears to set a child born to a man against a child born to a woman, but the sense cannot be securely recovered.
literal: One hears, it is born for a man; one hears, it is born for a woman.
usage: Unclear; the text as recorded is corrupt, so its use cannot be fixed.
igbo: A nụkata na-amụrụ nwoke a nụwa na-amụrụ nwaanyị

meaning: [uncertain] The line is obscure, but the image is a hand that has handled fish coming away scratched or roughened — apparently a remark that whoever does a job carries the marks of it.
literal: The hand that handles fish has grown nkụrụkụ (rough scrub).
usage: A doubtful line that a speaker would avoid; used, if at all, of someone visibly bearing the marks of the work they do.
igbo: Aka na-eme azụ gbaa nkụrụkụ

meaning: People get on by helping each other: the favour you do comes back to you, and no one manages alone.
equivalent: One hand washes the other.
literal: If the right hand washes the left hand, the left hand washes the right hand.
usage: Said to urge mutual help, or to remind someone that help given and help received go both ways.
igbo: Aka nri kwọọ aka ekpe, aka ekpe a kwọọ aka nri

meaning: The one through whom a child came into the world will not destroy that child; those who bear and raise a thing do not turn round and kill it.
literal: The hand of childbirth does not kill the child.
usage: Said to reassure that a parent or guardian will not harm the child, or to rebuke anyone scheming against what they themselves brought up.
igbo: Aka ọmụmụ anaghị egbu nwa

meaning: Once a person has his hand in the bag, it soon finds his own mouth — access to something is turned at once to one's own benefit.
literal: The hand has reached the bag, it has reached the mouth.
usage: Said when someone with control of shared goods or money quietly serves himself first, or as a dry comment on how people use what they can reach.
igbo: Aka ruru akpa, eru go ọnụ

meaning: Small amounts brought in again and again add up until there is enough; patient, repeated effort is what fills the mouth.
equivalent: Every little helps.
literal: Hand brings, hand brings, it fills the mouth.
usage: Used to encourage someone worn down by slow, small returns, or to value modest gifts and harvests for what they build up to.
igbo: Aka wete aka wete, o ju ọnụ

meaning: The akịdị bird does not know where one piece of land ends and another begins — said of a person with no sense of limits, who goes and takes where he has no right.
literal: The akịdị (small bird) does not know the boundary of the land.
usage: Said as a rebuke to someone overstepping his bounds, or with amusement about a restless wanderer who respects no boundary.
igbo: Akịdị anaghị ama oke ala

meaning: Good sense is what keeps a person alive; wisdom is life itself.
literal: Wisdom is life.
usage: Said to praise shrewdness, or to press someone to think carefully because sense is what preserves a person.
igbo: Ako bụ ndụ

meaning: [uncertain] The recorded line is broken and the sense cannot be recovered with confidence; the words concern weaving a bag and something done with a mat or bed.
literal: A bag is woven, and [unclear verb] on the mat.
usage: Not safely usable in speech; the text as recorded is corrupt.
igbo: Akpaa akpa, arụhụo n'ute

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo as recorded is unclear; the words seem to set weaving done out in the sun against eating while one is alive — perhaps that the labour a person does in his lifetime is what feeds him.
literal: Weaving (a bag) in the sun, one eats in life.
usage: Recorded text is too uncertain to recommend; if used, it would urge working while one still has life to work with.
igbo: Akpaa n'anwụ e rie na ndụ

meaning: Wealth is like water held in a gourd: it runs out here and reaches there, spreading to many places and many hands rather than staying in one spot.
literal: Wealth is like water in a gourd: it reaches here, it reaches there.
usage: Said about a rich person whose resources flow out to many people, or to note that wealth does not stay put.
igbo: Akụ dịka mmiri nọ n'ikwe, o ruga ebe a, o ruga ebe a

meaning: [uncertain] The line is unclear; the picture is of a bird of prey that wheels about in the sky and comes down at last on the frog's offspring — apparently about where power or fortune finally comes to rest.
literal: The akụ bird, having flown about, came down on the frog's child.
usage: Recorded text is uncertain; a speaker would reach for it, if at all, over a turn of fortune that lands on the least expected.
igbo: Akụ ferechaa ọ daara nwa awọ

meaning: When the finished thing is brought home everyone can see whose hands made it; a person's work shows plainly who did it.
literal: When the akụ/bag reaches home, the one who wove it is known.
usage: Said when the quality of someone's completed work reveals the hand behind it, whether to praise good work or shame poor work.
igbo: Akụ rue ụlọ a mara onye kpara ya

meaning: [uncertain] The recorded line is corrupt; it likens a story to a hole that is not opened or filled, but the intended point cannot be recovered with confidence.
literal: This story is a hole which does not open with ede (cocoyam).
usage: Not safely usable; the text as recorded is broken, though it is plainly a saying about tale-telling.
igbo: Akụkọ a bụ oghere ji egheghi ede

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo as recorded is unclear; it speaks of a new egg coming out of maamiri (water/spirit-water), but what the saying is meant to teach cannot be settled.
literal: A new egg is coming out of maamiri (water).
usage: Recorded text is too uncertain to recommend in speech.
igbo: Akwa ọhụrụ na-apụ maamiri

meaning: When the hen's egg is struck and breaks against the stone, it is the stone that is shamed — the blame for harm done in a clash falls on the strong, not on the one who is broken.
literal: The hen's egg knocked and cracked; shame came upon the stone.
usage: Said as consolation when the small and weak come off worst in a quarrel with the powerful, and to lay the fault where it belongs.
igbo: Akwa ọkụkọ tie akị, ihere emee nkume

meaning: Rare things are valued because they are rare; what we seldom see is admired all the more.
literal: The eye saw the eagle and admired it, because one does not see the eagle every day.
usage: Said when a rare person or achievement appears, to explain why everyone is making so much of it.
igbo: Anya hụrụ ugo jaa ya mma maka na a naghị ahụ ugo kwa daa

meaning: Time will show who is who; the true nature of each person eventually comes out.
literal: We will know the tortoise — the one that is a rat.
usage: Said when a group must wait and see which of them is trustworthy and what each person really is.
igbo: Anyị ga-ama mbe naabụ nke bụ oke

meaning: A jest or taunt lands on the sore spot; what is only a joke to everyone else wounds the one who is already hurting.
literal: Mockery stepped on a leg where there was no sore; if it is the person whose leg is sore, he weeps.
usage: Said when a remark that the whole gathering laughs at cuts one person in particular.
igbo: Ariri azọrọ ụkwụ ebeghi akwa, ọ bụrụ onye zọrọ ya ụkwụ na-ebe akwa

meaning: An evil that is tolerated long enough becomes accepted custom.
literal: When abomination fills the belly, it becomes tradition.
usage: A warning against letting a wrongdoing go unchallenged, because repetition will turn it into accepted practice.
igbo: Arụ gbaa afọ, o buru omenaala

meaning: An overreaching power is reminded of its origins and limits; no one is too big to be humbled.
literal: When the deity becomes too strong, one shows it the stick with which it was flogged.
usage: A warning to someone throwing his weight around that he can be reminded of where he came from.
igbo: Arụsị kpakarịa ike, e gosi ya osisi e jiri pịa ya

meaning: [uncertain] A corrupt or truncated line about ashịrị and ogoli; the sense cannot be recovered.
literal: Ashịrị finished ogoli; he carried up eju ọkụ.
usage: Cannot be quoted reliably; the line as recorded is damaged.
igbo: Ashịrị gụwa ogoli o bulie eju ọkụ

meaning: [uncertain] A child may turn out unlike its parent, as when a sheep bears a goat; the wording of the second half is unclear.
literal: The sheep bore a goat; it clapped hands to the child.
usage: Cannot be used with confidence; the recorded line is unclear.
igbo: Atụrụ mụrụ ebịla gba aka nwa

meaning: Someone imagines he is rebelling when he is only hurting himself; his defiance is empty.
literal: The sheep is licking its own tail; it thinks it is defying its owner.
usage: A mocking rebuke of someone who mistakes petty self-harm for rebellion.
igbo: Atụrụ na-anyụre ọdụ ya, o chee na ọ na-emegide onye nwe ya

meaning: When the moment of testing comes, the one without skill makes a clumsy showing.
literal: The sheep said that if drumming is played up to its home, if it does not know how to dance, it leaps up.
usage: A taunt at someone who lacks the skill for the occasion he has been called to.
igbo: Atụrụ sị na a kụrụ egwu ruo na be ya, ọ bụrụ na ọ maghị agba, ọ wụliwe elu

meaning: [uncertain] A fragment that cannot be reconstructed; the second half is not recoverable Igbo.
literal: Atụwa agba was seen; aba nshị.
usage: Cannot be quoted reliably; the line as recorded is damaged.
igbo: Atụwa agba ahụrụ, aba nshị

meaning: Nothing happens without a reason; when something unusual is done, there is a cause behind it.
literal: The toad does not run in the daytime for nothing.
usage: Said when someone behaves strangely and others want to know what is really behind it.
igbo: Awọ anaghị agba ọsọ ehihie na nkịtị

meaning: [uncertain] The frog speaks to its fellow frog in frog language; likely the line is truncated and the sense incomplete.
literal: The frog said to its fellow frog, 'wọmkọm.'
usage: Cannot be quoted reliably; the recorded line is fragmentary.
igbo: Awọ sị awọ ibe ya wọmkọm

meaning: [uncertain] Once a thing has been openly announced, it should not be secretly tampered with; the wording as recorded is unclear.
literal: The fish whose announcement is known, it is not good for the rat to bite it.
usage: Cannot be used with confidence; the recorded line is unclear.
igbo: Azụ a mara ọkwa ya ọ dịghị mma oke ịta ya

meaning: One grows great by consuming others; greatness in this world is often built at the expense of one's own fellows.
literal: The fish that does not swallow its fellow fish does not grow big.
usage: Said ruefully about the powerful who rise by preying on those around them.
igbo: Azụ na-eloghi ibe ya anaghị ebu

meaning: [uncertain] A corrupt, repeated line of uncertain reference ('nama'); no reliable sense can be given.
literal: Bring meat, bring meat — is it on the body of the nama?
usage: Cannot be quoted reliably; the line as recorded is damaged.
igbo: Beta anụ , beta anụ , ọ kwa n'ahụ nama

meaning: [uncertain] The palm kernel that is sold is the one that accepts the blame; the one who is traded away or offered up ends up carrying the guilt.
literal: The palm kernel that was sold is accepting the offense.
usage: Used when someone vulnerable or already compromised is made to bear blame for others.
igbo: Akwụ rere ere na ikwe mpu

meaning: One person's misfortune becomes another person's advantage; bad land is the titled elder's gain.
equivalent: One man's loss is another man's gain.
literal: Land that is not good is the benefit of the nze titleholders.
usage: Said when someone profits from a situation that harms someone else.
igbo: Ala adịghị mma bụ uru ndi nze

meaning: [uncertain] A tool that worked for a small task is being proposed for a bigger one; what sufficed for one thing may not suffice for another.
literal: The stick with which one saw a rat is known; one says use it to see kpalakuku.
usage: A warning not to assume that a method or instrument equal to a small challenge will handle a greater one.
igbo: Amara nkụ ahụ e jiri hụọ oke, sị were ya hụọ kpalakuku

meaning: As long as one survives, there is hope of enjoying good things; the one who does not die will yet eat meat.
equivalent: While there's life, there's hope.
literal: The creature that does not die [before] the sun sets will eat hairy meat.
usage: A consolation to someone enduring hardship, urging them to hold on.
igbo: Amụ na-anwụchụghị anwụchi ga-eri anụ gbara aji

meaning: One should not command another person's child; if the mother has not called him, the father should be the one to call him.
literal: I do not say a child should lift me onto the chair; if his mother has not called him, let his father call him.
usage: A reminder to respect parents' authority over their children rather than sending them on errands yourself.
igbo: Anaghị m asị nwata buliere m n'oche, nne ya akpọghị ya nna ya akpọọ ya

meaning: Bad behavior invites harsh consequences; an animal that runs wildly is shot with a harsh gun.
equivalent: As you sow, so shall you reap.
literal: If an animal runs a bad race, one shoots it with a bad gun.
usage: A warning that cruelty or recklessness will meet a fittingly severe response.
igbo: Anụ gbaa ajọ ọsọ, a gbaa ya ajọ egbe

meaning: When a quarrel or misfortune concerns others, an innocent bystander should not be dragged into it.
literal: The bee stings, the wasp stings; what has that joined to my puppy's eye?
usage: Said to refuse involvement in a dispute that has nothing to do with one.
igbo: Aṅụ gọọ, ebu gọọ, gịnị gbakpọkwaranụ nwa nkịta m anya

meaning: A loss or failure today need not be final; there is another opportunity tomorrow.
equivalent: Tomorrow is another day.
literal: The animal goes home today; tomorrow is hunting.
usage: A consolation after a setback, urging persistence.
igbo: Anụ laa taa echi bụ nta

meaning: The one who leads or arrives first gets the best share.
equivalent: First come, first served.
literal: The animal that leads the way drinks good water.
usage: Said to encourage initiative or to note the advantage of being first.
igbo: Anụ mbu ụzọ na-aṅụ mmiri ọma

meaning: If you follow someone whose nature is not yours, you will suffer for it; bad company or unsuitable imitation brings injury.
literal: The animal that follows the monkey sprains its leg.
usage: A warning against keeping company with or imitating those whose ways will lead you into trouble.
igbo: Anụ soro enwe o majie ụkwụ

meaning: [uncertain] A bite leaves a tooth mark, not a cure; harm should not be mistaken for help.
literal: The bite leaves the mark of teeth; it is like a tooth that treated an animal.
usage: A warning not to accept an attack as if it were kindness.
igbo: Anụta akara eze, ọ dịka eze ọ gwọrọ anụmanụ

meaning: One who has already done a terrible thing will go on to commit even greater sacrilege; wrongdoing escalates.
literal: The animal that bit a dog to death is committing a bad abomination.
usage: A warning that a person who crosses one line will not stop at worse.
igbo: Anụ tagburu nkịta na-ata ajọ arụ

meaning: Do not settle for an inferior thing when something better is on the way.
equivalent: Good things come to those who wait.
literal: Do not drink ngwo when nkwu is coming.
usage: A warning against impatiently taking a lesser option before the better one arrives.
igbo: Aṅụla ngwọ na nkwụ na-abịa

meaning: Ripeness or quality can be known by looking; observation reveals what is ready or good.
literal: It is with the eye that one knows ripe corn.
usage: Said when advising someone to observe carefully before judging or acting.
igbo: Anya ka e ji ama ọka chara acha

meaning: [uncertain] What my eyes have seen cannot be denied or called back; do not summon me as though I did not see.
literal: My eye saw you; do not call me.
usage: Used to insist on the evidence of one's own sight or to refuse being drawn into a matter one has witnessed.
igbo: Anya m hụrụ gị akpọla m

meaning: [uncertain] The line is a misspelled duplicate of 51947 and its sense is not settled; it looks to say that even the lowly locust, once it dances the otele, gives birth to cleverness — that cunning is born when a small creature is stirred into action.
literal: The agbịsị (locust) danced otele; it gave birth to wisdom.
usage: Used of a small or lowly person who shows surprising cunning once they are put on the spot, though the line is unreliable as given here.
igbo: Agbịsị gbaa otele ọ mụrụ akọ

meaning: Someone who has made herself fine and capable can afford to wait for a partner of equal worth — you are matched at the level you have prepared yourself for.
literal: A girl came and was well adorned; she waits for her mate.
usage: Said of a woman who holds out for a suitor who is her equal, or as advice to make something of yourself before expecting your peer.
igbo: Agbọghọbịa tochaa o chere ibe ya

meaning: [uncertain] The line reads as though a kindred busy with its own feasting has no time for the sick among them; the phrasing is awkward and no settled sense can be fixed for it.
literal: A kindred that eats ekpe does not treat the sick person.
usage: A speaker might reach for it to rebuke merrymakers who leave an ill person untended, but the line is unreliable.
igbo: Agbụrụ na-eri ekpe anaghị agwọ onye ọrịa

meaning: [uncertain] A respelling of 51944 and equally unsettled; it appears to say that even the lowly locust, once it dances the otele, gives birth to cleverness — small creatures show cunning when stirred into action.
literal: The agbụsị (locust) danced otele; it gave birth to wisdom.
usage: Offered of a small or lowly person who shows unexpected cleverness under pressure, though the line cannot be trusted as it stands.
igbo: Agbụsị gbaa otele ọ mụrụ akọ

meaning: [uncertain] Roughly: when fates clash no quarter is given to weakness — a contest of destiny does not spare the lame.
literal: A war of destiny does not eat lameness.
usage: Used of a hard contest or struggle in which the weak are shown no mercy.
igbo: Agha akara aka anaghị eri ngwọrọ

meaning: When the powerful arrive, the weak take to their heels — the strong clear the ground of everyone else.
literal: The leopard entered, the mgbada antelope took to running.
usage: Said when someone's arrival instantly scatters or silences those who cannot stand up to them.
igbo: Agụ bata mgbada awara ọsọ

meaning: If hunger can kill a rich man, it will drag the poor man away — the hardship that brings down the strong makes short work of the weak.
literal: Hunger killed the rich man; it got the poor man, it drags him.
usage: Said to show how much harder a general hardship bites for those with fewer means.
igbo: Agụọ gburu ogaranya nwete ogbenye ọ dọrie ya

meaning: Hunger that still has hope does not kill — as long as a person keeps hoping, hardship will not finish them off.
literal: Hunger that has hope does not kill and kill.
usage: A consolation to someone in want, urging them to hold on to hope.
igbo: Agụọ nwere olile anya anaghị egbu egbu

meaning: Good character is the best thing a person can have — best of all when it is inborn, moulded by nature rather than put on.
literal: Character is better, if Eke (the creator) moulded it.
usage: Said in praise of a person whose good character seems native to them rather than assumed.
igbo: Agwa ka mma ma eke tụa ya

meaning: [uncertain] A snake can only bring forth its own kind — whatever it bears will have a snake's tail; you cannot breed yourself out of your nature.
literal: A snake must not give birth to a thing that has a long tail.
usage: Used of children who turn out exactly like their parents, or of someone who cannot hide what they are.
igbo: Agwọ aghaghị imu ihe nwere ọdụ ogologo

meaning: [uncertain] The line looks truncated — 'the snake is in the akịrịka' — but if it stands as given it warns that danger is hiding close at hand, right beside you.
literal: The snake is in the akịrịka (thicket).
usage: Offered as a warning that something dangerous is lurking nearby, though the line is unreliable as recorded.
igbo: Agwọ dị n'akịrịka

meaning: If you will not act according to your nature, you will be treated with contempt — the snake that refuses to bite ends up as the string children tie firewood with.
literal: The snake did not do the thing with which it is a snake; children took it and tied firewood with it.
usage: A rebuke to someone who lets others ride roughshod over them instead of standing up for themselves.
igbo: Agwọ emeghị ihe o ji bụrụ agwọ ụmụ aka ewere ya kee nkụ

meaning: Whoever swallows up another's portion takes on that other's burden as well — greed leaves you dragging two tails.
literal: The snake swallowed its fellow; it has two tails.
usage: Said of someone whose greed for another's property lands them with more trouble than they can carry.
igbo: Agwọ loro ibe ya na-enwe ọdụ abụọ

meaning: An account grows in the telling: the snake one person saw and reported has become a python by the time it is retold.
literal: A snake that one person saw becomes eke (a python).
usage: Said to warn that a second-hand report has been blown up, or to greet a story with scepticism.
igbo: Agwọ otu onye hụrụ na-aghọ eke

meaning: [uncertain] The line is garbled; the likeliest sense is that one whose hand cannot reach his own leg cannot reach another's — a person who cannot help himself is in no position to help anyone else.
literal: The snake says: he whose hand did not reach his leg — it reached him.
usage: Used to chide someone who would set others' affairs right while neglecting his own.
igbo: Agwọ sị onye aka ya na-ekotereghi ụkwụ ya ekotere ya

meaning: Sleep cannot be forced; some things come only of their own accord, however hard a person pushes.
literal: One does not use strength to sleep.
usage: Said to someone straining after what only arrives on its own — rest, sleep, another's goodwill.
igbo: E jighi ike arahụ ụra

meaning: Do not bring a destructive means to bear on something already within your grasp — you will burn the very thing you are looking for.
literal: One does not use fire to look for the boil on the hand.
usage: A caution to someone reaching for drastic measures to secure what he already holds.
igbo: E jighi ọkụ achọ ihe agba n'aka

meaning: Do not use fire to search for what is already in your hand; the means you choose must not destroy the prize you seek.
literal: One does not use fire to look for what is in the hand.
usage: A warning against risking ruin in order to obtain what is already safely yours.
igbo: E jighi ọkụ achọ ihe eji n'aka

meaning: How bad a market day will be cannot be known first thing in the morning; wait for the day to unfold before judging it.
literal: One does not use the morning to know the badness of the market.
usage: Said to people passing judgement on a matter before it has had time to play out.
igbo: E jighi ụtụtụ ama njọ ahịa

meaning: [uncertain] The line looks corrupt, but it points at using a helper or tool that cannot do the work set for it.
literal: One used a dog; one did not use a monkey (ọgbụ).
usage: A rebuke to someone who has chosen a helper or method that cannot do the job.
igbo: E jiri nkịta ejighi ọgbụ

meaning: [uncertain] When a small portion is passed from hand to hand, it becomes plain who is favoured and who is passed over, and names begin to fly.
literal: A share was divided hand to hand; it was known who was called ashị.
usage: Said when a little is being shared out among many and old favouritism or grudges surface.
igbo: E kee oke n'aka n'aka, amara onye akpọrọ ashị

meaning: Respect paid to a person must reach those who stand with him; greet the masquerade, and its palm fronds are greeted too.
literal: One greets the masquerade, one greets its palm fronds.
usage: Used to remind someone that thanks or respect owed to one person extends to those around him.
igbo: E kele mmanwụ, ekele ụmụ nkwụ ya

meaning: Pamper a dependent and he may turn on you; the puppy carried against the body is the one that bites the hand.
literal: One carried the puppy against the body; it bit (ọgọdọ).
usage: A rebuke to someone whose kindness to a hanger-on has been repaid with insolence.
igbo: E kuru nwa nkịta na ahụ, ọ takaa ọgọdọ

meaning: Answer a greeting and faces brighten; courtesy returned keeps goodwill alive between people.
literal: One accepts a greeting, the face shines.
usage: An encouragement to answer greetings and keep warmth alive between people.
igbo: E kwe ekele, ihu asaa

meaning: [uncertain] The wording is unclear, but the sense is that a kindness done to a person in a wretched state may come back at the helper as harm.
literal: One gave a leper a hand; doing good, it bit him.
usage: A warning against putting yourself out for those who will turn on the helper.
igbo: E kwe onye ekpenta n'aka, ibi ọma agụwa ya

meaning: Trouble often starts with something small that was waved aside as beneath notice; the little pot left unwatched is the one that boils over.
literal: If one despises the little pot, it boils over onto the fire.
usage: A warning to someone dismissing a small matter as not worth his attention.
igbo: E lelịa nwa ite, ọ gbọnyụọ ọkụ

meaning: However venerable an elder seems, he too was once a baby at his mother's breast; age does not put anyone beyond the human lot, so the old are owed respect and no one should be mocked for being small.
literal: If one looks an elder in the mouth, it is as if he did not suckle his mother's breast.
usage: A rebuke to anyone who mocks or belittles an old person.
igbo: E lewe okenye anya n'ọnụ, ọ dị ka ọ ṅụghị ara nne ya

meaning: The withered tree is a picture of what can come to the flourishing one; another's fall is a warning to those still standing.
literal: If one looks at the tree that dried up, the living one would fall.
usage: Said when a death or disaster is treated as someone else's business, to remind the living it could be theirs.
igbo: E lewe osisi kpọrọ nkụ, nke dị ndụ a bụrụ daa

meaning: One glance at the waist can cost a goat — desire can rush a person into trouble that must be paid for.
literal: One looks at the waist, one kills a goat.
usage: A warning to a man whose eyes are roaming where they will cost him.
igbo: E lewe ukwu, egbuo eghu

meaning: When the body is buried, the grudge is buried with it; death ends the quarrels a person left behind.
literal: One buried the corpse, one buried the ill feeling.
usage: Said at a burial or after a death to quiet old bitterness against the one who has died.
igbo: E lie ozu, e lie ọnụma

meaning: [uncertain] Where the way is kept open and worked, the good thing follows; where the way lies cold and unused, nothing comes of it.
literal: If the path is eaten, the cow is eaten; but if the path is cold, no cow.
usage: Said when a person's gain depends on who has kept the road travelled, as in disputes over access and opportunity.
igbo: E liwe ụzọ liwe ehi, ma tọrọ ụzọ ghara ehi

meaning: Once the wrong has been repaid and amends made, the matter is closed and there is no more weeping over it.
literal: If it is done and it is paid back, it does not shed tears.
usage: A rebuke to someone who keeps grieving or grumbling after amends have already been made.
igbo: E mee e megwara anaghị agba anya mmiri

meaning: Do a thing at once and you keep trouble away; it is delay that lets the harm grow.
equivalent: A stitch in time saves nine
literal: If one does it quickly, one acts against disaster.
usage: Urged on a person who is putting off a small task, to warn that the delay will cost more.
