igbo: E mee ngwa ngwa e meghara ọdachi

meaning: Give way a little and the person comes back asking for more.
equivalent: Give him an inch and he'll take a mile
literal: If one allows it, it then wants an allowance.
usage: A warning against indulging someone even slightly, since each concession invites a larger demand.
igbo: E mee ya allow, ọ chọwa allowance

meaning: [uncertain] Whatever patience or treatment is given to one person's child must be given to the other's — the same measure for everyone.
literal: One did the same for Ogwugwu's child as for Anosike's child.
usage: Used to insist on even-handedness between children or dependants.
igbo: E menyere nwa ogwugwu, e menyere nwa anosike

meaning: [uncertain] A word or a dispute cannot be carved into pieces; it is not settled by splitting it up.
literal: There is no word that is cut and cut.
usage: Said when a quarrel is being picked apart instead of settled.
igbo: E nweghi okwu esewe esewe

meaning: Someone who has never been given freely does not take a gift as his own; the unexpected kindness makes him ask who it is meant for.
literal: If one gives a child something he did not expect, he asks that one tell him, give it to whom.
usage: Said of a person who meets kindness with suspicion rather than thanks.
igbo: E nye nwata ihe ọ na-atụbaghị anya ya, ọ jụọ sị a sị ya nye onye

meaning: Once a man has been given his fill, he no longer cares about the work he was doing.
literal: If the dibia's belly is filled, he flings the medicine leaves into the bad bush.
usage: A caution against paying a workman in full before the work is finished.
igbo: E nyejue dibịa afọ, ọkpara ahịhịa ọgwụ n'ajọ ọhịa

meaning: [uncertain] The words are too garbled to fix the point; it seems to speak of a sweetness or good thing recognised only from where one stood.
literal: One from the ushi saw at the ama the sweetness of the nshi.
usage: Used where the sense of a saying is being recalled only imperfectly.
igbo: E si n’ushi ahụrụ ama ụtọ nshị

meaning: [uncertain] So long as the matter is never opened up and aired, we stay unsettled and cannot go home.
literal: If it is not opened, we are in not returning home.
usage: Said when a family or meeting cannot disperse because one unspoken matter remains.
igbo: E siwe egheghi eghe, anyị nọ n'alaghị ala

meaning: When favour is shown to some while the one with nobody to speak for him is passed over, the forsaken is driven to despair.
literal: If one takes the pot's child off the fire, the orphan goes and kills himself in the yard.
usage: A reproach to those who favour some and leave the helpless to their own devices.
igbo: E siwe nwa ite n'okụ, nwa mgbei ejegbuo onwe ya n'ozi

meaning: [uncertain] The setting of the trap and the taking of the fish belong together; preparation and the catch are one thing.
literal: The ugba was spread, the fish was spread.
usage: Said about preparation and the result it brings.
igbo: E tere ụgba etere azụ

meaning: Praise a man for the brave thing he has done and he will go and do another.
literal: If one praises the strong man for what he did, he does another.
usage: Said to spur a man on by praising the deed he has already done.
igbo: E too dike na nke omere omekwa ozo

meaning: Praise a woman for the good turn she has done and she will do another.
literal: If one praises a woman who did the ndudu, she does another.
usage: Said to encourage a woman's continued good work by praising what she has already done.
igbo: E too nwaanyị gwọtara ndudu, ọ gwọta ọzọ

meaning: Punishment goes with comfort: the hand that corrects a child is followed by the hand that draws him back in.
literal: If one used the right hand to hit a child, it is with the left hand that one draws him close.
usage: Said about correcting a child, to remind the elder that discipline must end in reconciliation.
igbo: E were aka nri tie nwata ihe e were aka ekpe kpọkete ya

meaning: The steady walker will reach the very place the runner reached; quiet perseverance arrives at the same destination in the end.
literal: Where a person of running reached is where a person of walking will reach.
usage: Said to encourage someone slower or younger who keeps going while others have dashed ahead.
igbo: Ebe onye ọsọ ruru ka onye ije ga-eru

meaning: People end up going the way they have been leaning; a person's habits and inclinations decide where he finally lands.
literal: The place the tree leaned is where it falls.
usage: A caution to someone whose habits are steering him toward a bad end, or a comment on someone who has behaved true to form.
igbo: Ebe osisi kpọhuru ka ọ na-ada

meaning: A person's dignity and good name are the very things that shield him.
literal: The majesty of the leopard guards the leopard.
usage: Said to urge someone to protect their reputation, or to explain why a respected person was spared trouble.
igbo: Ebube agụ na-eche agụ

meaning: Nobody knows what the future holds; tomorrow is heavy with things not yet seen.
literal: Tomorrow is pregnant.
usage: Said when people are planning too confidently, or to steady someone anxious about what is coming.
igbo: Echi di ime

meaning: [uncertain] The kite has already taken its place at the kill — a plot or disaster is already in motion.
literal: The kite has already perched at the slaughter.
usage: Said as a warning that trouble has already been set going and cannot easily be stopped.
igbo: Egbe eberego na mgbagbu

meaning: [uncertain] The outcome of a deed points back to its source — when trouble breaks out, everyone can see where it started.
literal: If the gun kills a bird, one knows where it will cry.
usage: Said after a mishap, to point out the obvious cause of the trouble.
igbo: Egbe gbuo nku a mara ebe ọ ga-ebe

meaning: Natural enemies cannot be partners or share the same ground in peace.
literal: The kite and the chicken do not trade in the same market.
usage: Used to warn someone against trying to make allies or business partners of natural rivals.
igbo: Egbe na ọkụkọ anaghị azụkọ ofu ahịa

meaning: Those of the same kind do not squabble over what they share; each knows his own portion.
literal: The kite and the vulture do not struggle over food.
usage: Said when relatives or colleagues are being urged not to fight over what belongs to them all.
igbo: Egbe na udele anaghị azọ nri

meaning: [uncertain] Sharing a name, a place or a resemblance does not make a person your kin or your child.
literal: The kite's feather is not the kite's child.
usage: Said to someone who mistakes closeness or likeness for real kinship.
igbo: Egbe nkanka nku abuzịghị nwa egbe

meaning: [uncertain] When a once-great person comes down to the ground, even the lowly climb on top of him.
literal: When Egbelegbe drops to the ground, the woman climbs up on it.
usage: Said when a powerful person has fallen and lesser people now trample over him.
igbo: Egbelegbe daruo ala, nwaanyị arịa ya elu

meaning: A creature can starve in the middle of plenty; being surrounded by abundance is no use if you cannot reach it.
literal: The goat died in the yam barn — hunger killed it.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who complains of lack while sitting on plenty he cannot or will not touch.
igbo: Eghu nwụrụ n'ọba ji awụụ agụọ gburu ya

meaning: Money is a sharp blade: it can cut a path for you or cut you, and it must be handled with care.
literal: Money is a sharp knife.
usage: Said when money is being spoken of as a tool that can build or destroy.
igbo: Ego bụ mma dị nkọ

meaning: Wealth is found among thorns; you must endure pain and struggle before money comes to you.
literal: Money is in the thorn.
usage: Said to push someone on through hardship when money is the reward at the end.
igbo: Ego dị n'ogwu

meaning: [uncertain] Fear fills no one's belly; it only walks ahead of you, so go on and do the thing anyway.
literal: Fear does not strike the belly, it goes first.
usage: Said to someone hesitating out of fear, to push them into acting.
igbo: Egwu anaghị atụ afọ, o buru ụzọ

meaning: [uncertain] A person dances to the tune put in front of him; what is placed before someone is what he responds to.
literal: The dance that falls in front of the fish is how the fish dances.
usage: Said when something must be done openly, where the person it concerns can see it.
igbo: Egwu dara n'ihu azị ka azị na-ete

meaning: Trouble has already struck before the event even begins; the outcome is spoiled in advance.
literal: The dance has not yet started, the antelope has already broken a leg.
usage: Said when a plan or contest is doomed before it starts.
igbo: Egwu ebidobeghi, mgbada agbajigo ukwu rịị

meaning: Among equals, each is the one who trips the other; no one is above another.
literal: If the puppy's dance is played, the puppy is the one who fell on its fellow; its fellow fell on it.
usage: Said when equals trade blame or when no one can claim superiority.
igbo: Egwuru egwu nwa nkịta na nwa nkịta bụ onye daara ibe ya ibe ya daara ya

meaning: When someone lacks the natural means to help themselves, providence cares for them.
equivalent: God tempers the wind to the shorn lamb.
literal: A cow that has no tail, its chi is driving away flies for it.
usage: Said to comfort the vulnerable or to acknowledge divine help for the helpless.
igbo: Ehi na-enweghi ọdụ, chi ya na-achụrụ ijiji

meaning: The main point of a journey is to return home safely.
literal: Going and returning is the head of journey.
usage: Said to travelers or someone setting out on a trip.
igbo: Eje alọ bụ isi ije

meaning: Someone is suffering harm yet claims to be the one causing it; deluded bravado.
literal: The snail is burning, it says that it is quenching the fire.
usage: Said to mock a person who is being harmed but boasts of control.
igbo: Ejula na-ere ọkụ, sị na ya na-agbanyụ ọkụ

meaning: [uncertain] Thanks or recognition is given at the point of benefit, when the thing is being enjoyed.
literal: The greeting of the ụgụrụ is answered at the side of the fire.
usage: Said when gratitude is expressed at the moment of receiving a benefit.
igbo: Ekele ụgụrụ a na-ekwe ya na akụkụ ọkụ

meaning: Every matter reaches its conclusion; all things come to an end.
literal: All prayers ended in Amen.
usage: Said when a long discussion or affair finally concludes.
igbo: Ekpere niile biri n'Amen

meaning: A public signal summons the community to assemble.
literal: If the ekwe is struck, the ama is gathered.
usage: Said to describe how a call brings people together or a warning that a signal will be answered.
igbo: Ekwe kụọ, ama agbaa

meaning: A person who keeps refusing eventually consents at the appointed time.
literal: Refusal refusal is agreeing in the time agreed.
usage: Said when someone who persistently refused finally agrees.
igbo: Ekweghị ekweghị na-ekwe n'ụta ekwere

meaning: Do not underestimate anyone; even the lowly can cause trouble.
literal: If one despises a child, its pot boiled over on the fire.
usage: A warning against belittling others.
igbo: Elelịa nwa ite ya gbunyụọ ọkụ

meaning: Adversity forces adaptation; one side's skill sharpens the other's.
equivalent: Necessity is the mother of invention.
literal: Eneke ntị oba said that since the hunter learned to shoot without missing, it learned to fly without perching.
usage: Said when someone adapts cleverly to a threat.
igbo: Eneke ntị oba si kamgbe dinta mutara ịgba ehieghi ehie, ya muta ife ebenyeghi ebenye

meaning: Even a cherished responsibility can become a painful burden.
literal: Monkey carried its child on its back, it became an aching sore.
usage: Said when a loved one or duty becomes a source of pain.
igbo: Enwe kwọ nwa ya n'azụ ya ghọrọ ụtụ na-ara

meaning: Respect is due regardless of size or status.
literal: However small the deity is, it is carried with two hands.
usage: Said to urge respect for even the smallest person or thing.
igbo: Etu ọ sọrọ arusị pee mpe, aka abụọ ka eji ebu ya

meaning: [uncertain] This may concern rivalry or comparison in childbirth, but the sense is unclear.
literal: A big utu was used to bear a child; that of a neighbor will be named like an elephant.
usage: Unknown due to corruption.
igbo: Ewere nnukwu utu amụ nwa, nke onye ibi ga aha ka enyi

meaning: [uncertain] The saying seems to describe an unexpected humiliation or misfortune, but the exact sense is unclear.
literal: A goat has chewed for me igu on the head.
usage: Unknown due to corruption.
igbo: Ewu ataala m igu n'isi

meaning: [uncertain] A vulnerable creature like a chicken has no secure resting place and must be careful where it sleeps.
literal: If it is a chicken, the road has slept.
usage: A warning to the vulnerable to stay alert.
igbo: Burukwa ọkụkọ ụzọ lakpuo ụra

meaning: [uncertain] When one's personal god has consented, the matter is settled and will be heard again.
literal: If Chi asks, one hears again.
usage: Used to say that destiny's decision cannot be argued away.
igbo: Chi bọọ a nụ ọzọ

meaning: [uncertain] The same providence that gives a poor person something will also provide the means to use or prepare it.
literal: The chi that gave the poor child yam will give him [mbazụ] that he will use to [egwuru] it.
usage: A consolation that God supplies not only the gift but also the way to make use of it.
igbo: Chi nyere nwa ogbenye ji ga-enye ya mbazụ ọ ga-eji egwuru ya

meaning: What is hot will cool; time and patience calm even fierce trouble.
literal: Chinchi told her children that what is hot will cool.
usage: A consolation to endure a heated moment, knowing it will pass.
igbo: Chinchi sị ụmụ ya ihe dị ọkụ ga jụ oyi

meaning: If you are looking for something, search where you last used it.
literal: If you search for your cloth, [search] where you bathed.
usage: Advising someone to retrace their steps instead of searching at random.
igbo: Chọwa akwa gi ebe ị sara ahụ

meaning: A healer who can cure otoro does not hang his power on the wall; he uses it.
equivalent: Don't hide your light under a bushel.
literal: The dibia treating otoro, has he hung his power on the wall?
usage: Urging someone to put their skill or resources to use rather than keeping them idle.
igbo: Dibịa na-agwọ otoro, o dewere ike ya n'uko?

meaning: [uncertain] Even a hero is subject to ordinary bodily weakness; strength does not exempt anyone from common frailty.
literal: A hero eats palm kernel; his body [ikikere].
usage: A reminder that no one, however strong, is above small human weaknesses.
igbo: Dike taa akị, ahụ ikikere ya

meaning: Do not let a helpful servant's usefulness make you give it a status it does not have; keep roles clear.
literal: The hunter will not say, because of the big dog that caught meat for him, [that] it should be called his mother's husband.
usage: Cautioning against misplaced familiarity or excessive praise for a helper.
igbo: Dinta agaghị asi maka oke nkịta jideere ya anụ kpọọ ya di nne ya

meaning: A wise diviner does not reveal everything he knows.
literal: Diochi does not finish saying everything he saw on the palm tree.
usage: Advising discretion and restraint in what one discloses.
igbo: Diochi anaghị ekwucha ihe niile ọ hụrụ n'elu nkwụ

meaning: [uncertain] The saying seems to claim that no one who has gone and heard can avoid returning; perhaps about the pull of home or destiny.
literal: Leave me, it is ure; there is no one who went and heard and did not return.
usage: Expressing that one cannot escape one's origin or fate.
igbo: Dupu m bụ ure, o nweghi onye lawara nụ ma ghara ilarụ

meaning: Another person's burden feels light because it is not your own; people do not feel another's grief as deeply.
literal: If one carries another person's corpse, it is like carrying a bundle of firewood.
usage: Rebuking those who are indifferent to another's suffering.
igbo: E buru ozu onye ọzọ, ọ dịka ebu ukwu nkụ

meaning: If you pay attention, you can detect approaching danger.
literal: If one puts an ear to the ground, one hears the sound of the feet of agbụsi.
usage: Urging vigilance and attentiveness to early signs of trouble.
igbo: E che nti n’ala, a nụ ụda ụkwụ agbụsi

meaning: When fighting breaks out, the coward runs.
literal: If war is fought, the coward runs.
usage: Rebuking cowardice or predicting who will flee in a crisis.
igbo: E gboo ọgụ, onye ụjọ a na-aba

meaning: A parent's love and concern for their child persist even in death.
literal: They shot the egbe ehi; its eyes will still be on the nwa shiishii.
usage: Praising a parent's enduring care for their child.
igbo: E gbugodiri egbe ehi, anya ya ka ga-adịkwa na nwa shiishii

meaning: If you destroy your strong person in a domestic quarrel, you will have to look for a hero when a real public war comes.
literal: If a hero is killed in a home war, when it reaches a public war, they will look for a hero.
usage: Warning against wasting one's defenders on internal strife.
igbo: E gbuo dike n'ọgụ ụlọ, e rue n'ọgụ ama achọwa dike

meaning: [uncertain] A deed done in hot anger comes out crooked: the killing is done while the temper is still up, and even the burial is left half-finished.
literal: One kills while still angry; one buries but the head.
usage: Said to check someone who wants to act at once on a hot temper, warning that the deed will come out botched.
igbo: E gbuo ma iwe, e lie ma isi

meaning: [uncertain] Settling a quarrel takes two clearings: the road ahead must be opened and the grievance in the mouth cleared as well.
literal: One clears the path; one clears the mouth.
usage: Used while peace is being made, when both the obstacle and the hard words have to be dealt with.
igbo: E gupee ụzọ, e gupee ọnụ

meaning: Worth shows on the outside: you can tell a cob of maize is full simply by looking at it.
literal: It is with the eye that one knows the maize cob that has formed fully.
usage: Said when a person's quality or readiness is plain to see and needs no testing or argument.
igbo: E ji anya ama ọka kara aka

meaning: Dangerous sweetness is paid for with your own head — a person finds out how sweet poison is at his own cost.
literal: It is with the head that one sees the sweetness of poison.
usage: A warning to someone drawn toward something sweet that will destroy him.
igbo: E ji isi ahụrụ ama ụtọ nsi

meaning: [uncertain] A person eats out of the mortar he pounds in — you live by the very thing you work with.
literal: One uses a mortar to eat a mortar.
usage: Said of someone whose labour and livelihood are one and the same thing.
igbo: E ji okwe eri okwe

meaning: If a strong man is put down but matters are not settled with him, the real trouble begins when he stands up again.
literal: They hold a strong man on the ground and have not settled with him well; that is now the time he has stood up.
usage: A warning to those who humiliate the powerful without making peace while they have them down.
igbo: E jide dike n'ala ma e kwotaghị ya mma, ọ bụzi mgbe o biliri ọtọ

meaning: Having the thing in hand is what lets a person speak with authority — the one holding the yam is the one who tells how ụganị tastes.
literal: One holds a piece of yam in the hand and uses it to tell the story about ụganị.
usage: Said when someone speaks on a matter because he has the very thing itself in hand.
igbo: E jide ibe ji n’aka e were kọwa akụkọ maka ụganị

meaning: [uncertain] Ability that is never shown gets written off — leave the gun unhandled and people will say a woman cannot fire it.
literal: The gun was not held properly, and one says that a woman will not eat it.
usage: Said of someone whose strength is doubted only because he has never had to display it.
igbo: E jidebeghi egbe, a na-ekwu na nwaanyị agaghị eri ya

meaning: [uncertain] Hoping is not a night-time affair: a person does not keep vigil over what he is waiting for; the night is for rest.
literal: One does not use the night to look forward in hope with the eye.
usage: Said to someone lying awake nursing an expectation, sending him to sleep and to leave it for daylight.
igbo: E jighi abalị arọ anya

meaning: [uncertain] Small means are not for sweeping away great things — you do not take a little snare to a rich man's great trap.
literal: One does not use a snare to throw away a rich man's big trap.
usage: Said when someone tackles a large matter with a puny tool or a trifling reason.
igbo: E jighi akpata atụfuo aba ọgaranya

meaning: [uncertain] You do not get into the prayer gathering on the strength of a friendly eye — favour and fine looks carry no weight there.
literal: One does not use a good eye to enter the prayer gathering.
usage: Said to someone who expects the assembly to favour him because of who he is.
igbo: E jighi anya ọma aba ụka ekpere

meaning: What lies in your own hand needs no mirror — nobody holds up a glass to see what he is already holding.
literal: One does not use a mirror to look at the thing held in the hand.
usage: Said to someone who goes by roundabout means to reach something plainly before him.
igbo: E jighi enyo ele ihe agba n'aka

meaning: [uncertain] You cannot talk a man out of what he is — no amount of Igbo speech will turn him into a white man.
literal: One does not use Igbo to tell him that he is a white man.
usage: Said when words are being used to dress a person up as something he is not.
igbo: E jighi igbo agwa ya onye ọcha

meaning: What is put into the ear is not put into the eye — words given in confidence are not to be shown around.
literal: One does not use the thing that is put into the ear to put into the eye.
usage: A rebuke to someone who carries a private word out into the open.
igbo: E jighi ihe a na-agba na ntị agba n'anya

meaning: [uncertain] Shame is no way to swallow a hardship — hiding your face will not get the trouble down; it has to be faced.
literal: One does not use shame to swallow a trial.
usage: Said to urge someone who keeps quiet out of shame to speak up about what is troubling him.
igbo: E jighi ihere elo anwa

meaning: Work done in good time is not wasted — sooner or later there will be need of what you have prepared.
literal: If one used the morning to draw water, does it look as though it will not be drunk?
usage: Said to nudge someone who is putting off a task, or to answer anyone asking why you are starting so early.
igbo: E were ụtụtụ kụta mmiri ụgụrụ ọ dị ka agaghị aṅụ ya aṅụ

meaning: [uncertain] The vulture is eaten by its name and not by its flesh — what is at stake in this line is reputation rather than substance, and the second half is obscure.
literal: That it reached where the vulture's name is eaten, it has perched on ngịga.
usage: Reached for when talk turns on a person's name growing larger than the facts about him.
igbo: E zue ka aha eri udele atọtuo ngịga

meaning: A person should act and spend only up to the limit of what he actually has.
equivalent: Cut your coat according to your cloth.
literal: Where the hand reaches is where the woman hangs her bag.
usage: A caution to someone attempting more than his means allow, or a defence of living modestly.
igbo: Ebe aka ruru nwaanyị ka ọ na-ekonye akpa ya

meaning: Even the person you lean on will carry you only as far as your own reach — support does not stretch beyond your own effort.
literal: Where the hand reaches, ogoli, is where she leans against her husband.
usage: Said of someone expecting more from a spouse or helper than that person's support can bear.
igbo: Ebe aka ruru ogoli, ka ọ na-tụkwasị di ya

meaning: [uncertain] When the place you are bound for is close at hand, no great struggle or preparation is called for — nearness spares effort.
literal: Where the land is near, one does not do wrestling.
usage: Said when someone makes heavy preparations for something already within reach.
igbo: Ebe ala dị nso anaghị eshi agụgọ mgba

meaning: When two people settle a matter between themselves in private, no outsider can say what really passed — only they and their gods know.
literal: Where two heads eat together, only their chi knows who washed the soup.
usage: Said when neighbours begin taking sides in a quarrel whose details were never witnessed by anyone else.
igbo: Ebe ndị isi abụọ na-eriko nri, naani chi ha ma onye gwọrọ ofe

meaning: The end does not wait for you to finish enjoying yourself — while a man is still filling his belly, his burial is already being arranged.
literal: While the cricket is still filling its stomach, its corpse is being brought out.
usage: A sobering remark dropped when someone is deep in pleasure or plenty.
igbo: Ebe nwanza na-eriju afo ka a na-ebuta ozu ya

meaning: As soon as you show you can carry something small, a heavier load is brought for you — capacity draws responsibility.
literal: While the child is carrying a snail, the head pad is being brought for him.
usage: Said half in praise, half in complaint, of a capable person whose competence keeps attracting more work.
igbo: Ebe nwata na-ebute ejula ka a na-ebute okpokoro isi ya

meaning: [uncertain] As soon as a child can shoulder the smallest load, the head pad for a bigger one is brought out — ability invites a heavier burden.
literal: While the child is carrying the corpse of nchi, the head pad is being brought for him.
usage: Used, like its twin, of someone whose usefulness keeps earning him more to carry.
igbo: Ebe nwata na-ebute ozu nchi ka a na-ebute okpokoro isi ya

meaning: A person keeps going back to the place where he gets something for himself; his interest sets his direction.
literal: Where the child gathers kernels, that is where he goes.
usage: Said of somebody whose repeated visits make his motives plain to everyone.
igbo: Ebe nwata na-atụtụta aki okpokoro ka ọ na-aga

meaning: In the hour of need there may be nobody at hand, not even a mother or a father — a person has to be able to stand on his own.
literal: Where the child cries and begs for a hand, his mother is not there for him, his father is not there for him.
usage: A hard consolation to someone left to cope alone, or a warning not to count on others.
igbo: Ebe nwata na-ebe akwa arụ aka, nne ya anọghi ya nna ya anọrọ ya

meaning: [uncertain] Good fortune shows in a person — the child with oil on his mouth is the one who steps out cheerfully.
literal: Where a child brings out an oily mouth, that is where he goes out rejoicing.
usage: Said of someone whose wellbeing is plain to everyone in the way he carries himself.
igbo: Ebe nwata na-ebuta ọnụ mmanụ ka ọ na-apụ ọrịrị

meaning: Whoever has been burned clings to the stone that shields him and will not let it go — a hard lesson teaches a person to hold fast to what protects him.
equivalent: A burnt child dreads the fire.
literal: When the fire burned the tortoise, it covered itself with a stone; now, is it a chicken carrying a fat leg that it will let go?
usage: Said of someone whose caution after a bad experience looks excessive to those who did not suffer it.
igbo: Ebe ọkụ gbara mbe ji okwute kwara akwa, ọ bụzi ọkụkọ bu ukwu abụba ka ọ ga-ahapụ?

meaning: [uncertain] The line breaks off before the point is made; as far as it goes it speaks of fire reaching the coconut — nothing is so sheltered that trouble cannot touch it.
literal: Where the fire served the coconut ...
usage: Not safely usable as it stands; the proverb appears cut short.
igbo: Ebe ọkụ nyụrụ awusa ọwa

meaning: Where a person lives is where he must also relieve himself — you cannot keep your own home at arm's length, and must take it with its good and its bad.
literal: Where a person lives is where he defecates.
usage: Said to someone who grumbles about his town or household and yet will not leave it.
igbo: Ebe onye bi ka ọ na-awachi

meaning: [uncertain] A person who lacks sense grows stubborn in it; foolishness hardens a person beyond correction.
literal: The goat makpu amakpu has hardened its bone.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who refuses to listen or be corrected.
igbo: Ewu makpu amakpu makpugodoro ọkpụkpọ ya

meaning: The will may be there, but nature or physical limitation can hold one back from the deed.
literal: The goat is doing a race, but hair did not allow it.
usage: Said when someone wants to act but is held back by their own limitations.
igbo: Ewu na ọshishiọ na-eme, kama ajị ekweghi ya

meaning: The young depend on their elders for provision; they watch the provider's mouth for what they need.
literal: The goat is chewing agbara; its child is looking at it in the mouth.
usage: Used to describe dependents waiting on a provider, or to remind providers of their responsibility.
igbo: Ewu na-ata agbara, nwa ya ana-ele ya anya n'ọnụ

meaning: Hearing about food does not satisfy hunger; knowing of plenty is not the same as having it.
literal: The goat that hears people cooking food, hunger is killing it.
usage: Said of someone who longs for what others have but cannot obtain it.
igbo: Ewu nnụ mmadụ na-akwara nri, agụrụ na-egbu ya

meaning: [uncertain] Hearing people eat does not feed you; longing for what others have leaves one hungry.
literal: The goat that hears people chewing food is dying in hunger.
usage: Used to pity or rebuke someone who envies what others enjoy but has none.
igbo: Ewu nnụ mmadu na-akwatara iri na-anwụ n'agụọ

meaning: For a poor person, a goat is as valuable as a cow; small resources are great wealth to the needy.
literal: A poor person's goat is his cow.
usage: Used to console or encourage someone who has little, pointing to the worth of what they have.
igbo: Ewu nwa ogbenye bụ ehi ya

meaning: If someone perishes amid plenty, lack is not what killed them; failure in a place of resources is not due to deprivation.
literal: The goat that died in a yam barn, it was not hunger that killed it.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who fails despite having every resource, or to note that opportunity was not the problem.
igbo: Ewu nwụrụ n'oba ji abụghị agụrụ gburu ya

meaning: [uncertain] The saying seems to warn that a ruler who cannot be told or advised is a dangerous thing.
literal: King, the one who should not tell me is nshị in ọgọdọ akpagharị.
usage: Used as a warning against refusing advice, especially by someone in authority.
igbo: Eze onye agwala m bu nshị n'ọgọdọ akpagharị

meaning: Hard times are followed by better times; a good dry season brings a good rainy season.
equivalent: After a storm comes a calm.
literal: A good dry season brings a good rainy season.
usage: Used to console someone enduring hardship, assuring them relief will follow.
igbo: Ezigbo ọkọchị na-eweta ezigbo udu mmiri

meaning: Good words are never in short supply; wise speech is always available.
literal: A good word has no scarcity.
usage: Used to encourage someone to seek or speak good counsel.
igbo: Ezigbo okwu enweghi osịsa

meaning: Truth is life itself; living in truth is what sustains a person.
literal: Truth is life.
usage: Used to affirm honesty and truthfulness as essential to a good life.
igbo: Eziokwu bụ ndụ

meaning: The priest prayed in Latin, and the people, not understanding it, thought it was all Amen; people often follow what they do not understand.
literal: Father prayed Latin, where we thought it was in Amen.
usage: Used to mock blind following or the pretense of understanding.
igbo: Father sụrụjuo Latin, ebe anyị chere ya bụ n' Amen

meaning: [uncertain] Go back to your own place; settle where you belong and have a claim.
literal: Go and spread your cloth where you washed your body.
usage: Used to dismiss someone back to their own home or business.
igbo: Gaa chịrị akwa gị ebe ị sara ahụ

meaning: [uncertain] A defiant challenge: do your worst; I will not be moved.
literal: Kick me with foot in the teeth.
usage: Used as a bold challenge or refusal to be intimidated.
igbo: Gbaa m ụkwụ n'eze

meaning: [uncertain] One who refuses to lend a hand cannot share in the honor; you and the non-contributor have no part in the success.
literal: You and the person who does not put hand in strength come out from the nose.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who will not contribute but expects the benefit.
igbo: Gị na onye na-aghịnye aka n'ike esi n'imi

meaning: A burden carried together does not weigh anyone down.
equivalent: Many hands make light work.
literal: A load that is ours does not weigh down.
usage: Said to rally others to a task that is too heavy for one person alone.
igbo: Ibu anyị danda

meaning: When the dancers lose their step, the whole dance is spoiled — one careless participant ruins what everyone shares.
literal: Dancing spoils, the dance spoils.
usage: Aimed at someone whose carelessness is putting a shared effort at risk.
igbo: Ịgba dagharịa, egwu dagharịa

meaning: [uncertain] The line is truncated and its sense cannot be recovered; as written it says the sky (or a titled man, Igwe) has gone off somewhere.
literal: Igwe has gone to that place.
usage: Not reliably usable; the saying survives only as a fragment.
igbo: Igwe ejee ngaa

meaning: What is scraped from the side of the pot reaches the side of the mouth — the small things a person gathers by their own effort still end up feeding them.
literal: What is scraped at the side of the pot lands at the side of the mouth.
usage: Offered to console or encourage someone whose small, patient gains look like nothing.
igbo: Ihe a kpachatara n'akụkụ ite na-ala n'akụkụ ọnụ

meaning: What you hunt for in the loft turns out to be down at ground level — the thing you seek far away is usually close at hand.
literal: The thing that is sought in the upper roof is seen in the lower roof.
usage: A gentle rebuke to someone who overlooks the obvious and searches everywhere else.
igbo: Ihe a na-achọ n'uko elu ka ahụrụ n'uko ala

meaning: A snake's young will grow long no matter what — children turn out like their parents; nature shows itself in the end.
equivalent: The apple doesn't fall far from the tree.
literal: What a snake bore must grow long.
usage: Said when a child's behaviour plainly repeats the parent's, whether in praise or in reproach.
igbo: Ihe agwọ mụrụ aghaghị ito ogologo

meaning: What a rich man has planted in his heart is his own secret — the wealthy keep their true intentions to themselves.
literal: The thing planted in a rich man's heart.
usage: A caution offered to someone putting trust in a wealthy man's promises.
igbo: Ihe akọ n'obi ọgaranya

meaning: [uncertain] What is born is born and what is bought is bought — most likely marking the difference between a child of one's own blood and a person or thing acquired.
literal: A thing born is born, a thing bought is bought.
usage: Turns up in talk about kinship, adoption or loyalty, but the sense is not securely fixed.
igbo: Ihe amụrụ amụ ka ihe agwọrọ agwọ

meaning: [uncertain] The line is corrupt and doubles a variant of a similar proverb; nothing beyond its reference to buying in the market can be safely drawn from it.
literal: The thing that is ogoli — buy it in the market.
usage: Not safely usable in speech as the text stands.
igbo: Ihe awọrọ ogoli azụa n'ahịa

meaning: What falls into the water must be felt for with the feet — when sight fails you, you use whatever means are left.
literal: The thing that fell into the water, it is feet that are used to look for it.
usage: Said when someone has to manage with poor tools in a murky or hopeless-looking situation.
igbo: Ihe dabara na mmiri, ụkwụ ka eji achọ ya

meaning: [uncertain] The wording is obscure (the second householder is not identifiable) and appears to say that the same lot is found in one house as in another.
literal: What is at the rat's place is at the ọgịnị's place.
usage: Recorded here as a doubtful line; a speaker would be unlikely to reach for it.
igbo: Ihe dị be oke dị be ọgịnị

meaning: Good things belong to the living — only one who is alive can enjoy what is good.
literal: A good thing is with an eye that is alive.
usage: A consolation to the living when talk turns to the dead and to what they have lost.
igbo: Ihe dị mma na anya gbara ndụ

meaning: [uncertain] A corrupt doubling of the preceding proverb; only the mention of buying in the market can be made out, and the sense is unrecoverable.
literal: That thing is wọrọ ogori — it has been bought in the market.
usage: Not safely usable in speech as the text stands.
igbo: Ihe ahụ di wọrọ ogori azụọla n’ahịa

meaning: [uncertain] What sets the dibia above his rivals comes down to the leaf he needs — a practitioner's standing rests on the materials of his craft.
literal: The thing the dibia used to surpass his fellow in anger is the want of leaves.
usage: Used when a person's advantage, or their grievance, traces back to the tools of their trade.
igbo: Ihe dibịa jiri kara ibe iwe bụ na mkpa akwụkwọ

meaning: The funeral food tastes sweet to a fool, but once he has eaten his fill and stands up he is back to his own troubles — comfort got at another's expense does not last.
literal: The thing used to bury a corpse pleases the fool, but when he has eaten it up and rises.
usage: A jab at someone who lives off others' misfortunes and forgets he must go home afterwards.
igbo: Ihe e ji eli ozu na-atọ ofeke ụtọ, ma ya rịachaa ya bilite

meaning: A child takes after its parent; you cannot expect a hawk's offspring to turn out to be a chicken.
equivalent: The apple doesn't fall far from the tree.
literal: What the egbe gave birth to cannot be a chicken.
usage: Said when a child behaves exactly like a parent, or to reject the hope that someone will not follow family nature.
igbo: Ihe egbe mụrụ aghaghị ibu ọkụkọ

meaning: Different creatures react differently to the same danger: what makes the strong flee may only leave the weak staring.
literal: What the cow saw and ran from, the chicken saw and is astonished.
usage: Used when people respond very differently to the same event or threat.
igbo: Ihe ehi hụrụ gbaa ọsọ, ka ọkụkọ hụrụ na-atụ ọnụ

meaning: When a container is full, it is closed; when a person has had enough, they should stop and keep quiet.
literal: What filled a bag, one tied its mouth.
usage: A caution against greed or overreaching, urging someone to stop once they have enough.
igbo: Ihe ju akpa e kechie ya ọnụ

meaning: [uncertain] The proverb is garbled or truncated; its sense cannot be reliably recovered.
literal: What is more than a mat met a mat in the mouth.
usage: Unclear; the line is too corrupt to use confidently.
igbo: Ihe ka nte bakwutere nte n'ọnụ

meaning: Nothing stands by itself; whatever stands has something placed beside or beneath it, so no one succeeds without support.
literal: What stood, what was placed beside it.
usage: Said to remind someone that their standing depends on others.
igbo: Ihe kwụrụ, ihe akwụdebe ya

meaning: [uncertain] The proverb is obscure or corrupt; its sense cannot be reliably recovered.
literal: What happened that made ede cut nwịị.
usage: Unclear; the line is too corrupt to use confidently.
igbo: Ihe mere ede jiri bee nwịị

meaning: Whoever causes a condition shares in its consequences; the man responsible for a pregnancy also bears its burdens.
literal: What bites a pregnant woman also bites the one who put it in her.
usage: Used to remind a man that he shares responsibility for the trouble he has caused.
igbo: Ihe na-agụ nwaanyị dị ime na-agụkwa onye tụbara ya

meaning: Pleasurable things can be harmful or deadly; what is sweet may destroy.
literal: What is sweet is killing.
usage: A warning against being led by pleasure without seeing its danger.
igbo: Ihe na-ato ụtọ na-egbu egbu

meaning: Some make a loud noise at danger, while others noticed it long before and quietly escaped; quiet wisdom acts earlier than noisy alarm.
literal: What the dog saw and barked at, the sheep saw long ago and ran quietly.
usage: Said when someone belatedly reacts noisily to what a wiser person had already avoided.
igbo: Ihe nkịta hụrụ gbọwa ụja, atụrụ a hụla kemgbe gba nkịtị

meaning: What you do for or to another comes back to you; the treatment you give your neighbor becomes your own fate.
equivalent: What goes around comes around.
literal: What a man gave his fellow is what caught me.
usage: A warning that kindness or cruelty to others returns to the giver.
igbo: Ihe nwoke nyere ibe ya bụ ngaa jidere m

meaning: [uncertain] The proverb's sense is obscure; it seems to say that something seen by a lowly person is seen also by a mother hen, but the exact point is not clear.
literal: What ofeke saw is what the hen brooding chicks saw.
usage: Unclear; not reliably usable without more context.
igbo: Ihe ofeke hụrụ bụ ihe ọkụkọ chị ụmụ hụrụ

meaning: If a bad practice is allowed to continue long enough, people come to accept it as custom.
literal: If evil lasts a year, it becomes custom.
usage: A warning against tolerating wrongdoing until it becomes tradition.
igbo: Ihe ọjọọ gbaa afọ, ọ bụrụ omenaala

meaning: Experience sees farther than youth: an elder seated can perceive what a child standing cannot.
literal: What an elder sitting down saw, a child standing up will not see it.
usage: Said to urge respect for the insight of elders over the confidence of the young.
igbo: Ihe okenye nọdịrị ala hụ, nwata kwụrụ ọtọ ọ gaghị ahụ ya

meaning: [uncertain] The line is corrupt or fragmentary; its sense cannot be reliably recovered.
literal: What the chicken knows, water achụ it needs.
usage: Unclear; too corrupt to use confidently.
igbo: Ihe ọkụkọ ma mmiri achụ dị ya mkpa

meaning: A dog answers to the name its owner gives it; people too respond according to how they are addressed or treated.
literal: What a person called his dog is what it is answering.
usage: Said to show that the way you name or address someone shapes how they respond.
igbo: Ihe onye kpọrọ nkịta ya ka ọ na-aza

meaning: There is no death without a cause — even a mere puppy does not simply die; look for the reason before you accept that a thing just happened.
literal: What did the puppy use to die?
usage: Said when someone insists an event was random or refuses to ask why it happened.
igbo: Gịnị jikwanụ nwa nkịta ọnwụ?

meaning: [uncertain] The line is fragmentary, but as it stands it says that people who have one affliction have another keeping it company — trouble arrives in company.
literal: They have ebu; they have mfụ.
usage: Cited, rarely and mostly in the shortened form, when one trouble is found to have brought another with it.
igbo: Ha nwere ebu nwee mfụ

meaning: [uncertain] What is written on the outside of a vehicle is not the journey; leave the inscription alone and get inside — the label is not the thing.
literal: Leave the thing written on the motor, enter the motor.
usage: Said when someone judges a person or a thing by the writing on the outside of it.
igbo: Hapu ihe e dere na motor banye motor

meaning: [uncertain] Everything that happened in the night, leave it to the mosquitoes — the night's business stays with the small things that witnessed it.
literal: Leave everything that happened at night, let it be mosquitoes.
usage: Said when something was done quietly in the dark and the speaker wants it left where it was done.
igbo: Hapu ihe niile bere n'abalị ka ọ bụrụ anwụnta

meaning: [uncertain] The line is too short to fix a sense with certainty; it reads as an instruction to throw or aim seven times at the eye, most likely counsel to keep at a thing.
literal: Throw seven into the eye.
usage: Recited as an encouragement not to give up after repeated misses.
igbo: Hie asaa n'anya

meaning: Poverty that outlasts you: you will be a poor man here and still a poor spirit after — want follows a person past the grave.
literal: You will be poor, and be a spirit.
usage: A grim remark about someone whose poverty looks as though even death will not end it.
igbo: Ị ga abụ ogbenye bụrụ amụsu

meaning: [uncertain] The knife and the yam serve whoever the hand cuts for — what a person holds goes to the one he chooses to give it to.
literal: You have a knife and a piece of yam; the one you sliced it for eats it.
usage: Said when help or goods are seen to favour one person over another at the giver's choosing.
igbo: I ji mma jiri ibe ji, onye ị waranyere ya rie

meaning: If you have turned down the dog's head, what is the jaw to you? — refusing the whole makes the parts worth nothing to you.
literal: If you refuse the dog's head, what will you use its jaw to do?
usage: A rebuke to someone who has turned down the main offer and now haggles over the scraps.
igbo: Ị jụta ishi nkịta, I were agba ya mee gịnị?

meaning: You are driving the puppy off the filth — will you eat it? — do not grudge another what you yourself would never touch.
literal: You are chasing the puppy away from the faeces; will you eat it?
usage: A rebuke to someone who stops others from enjoying what he would never touch himself.
igbo: Ị na achụpụ nwa nkịta na nshi, ị ga eri ya?

meaning: Are you laughing at me because I look strange? — there is nothing odd on me for you to mock.
literal: You are laughing at me; do I have feathers on my back?
usage: Said back to someone laughing at you for no reason, demanding to know what is so odd about you.
igbo: Ị na-achị m ọchị, eyi m azụ efe?

meaning: To behave as though the Holy Spirit were not God — to act as if the power over you were of no account.
literal: You are acting as if the Holy Spirit is not God.
usage: A rebuke to someone who carries on as if a power above him did not exist or did not matter.
igbo: Ị na-emezi ka mmụọ nsọ abụrọ Chukwu

meaning: [uncertain] Sitting at ease counting lizards while the tail refuses — the tally fails on the detail you did not reckon with; plans made in comfort are ruined by the one thing that will not cooperate.
literal: You are sitting down counting lizards, but the tail does not agree with it.
usage: A mild rebuke to someone spinning plans that one small uncooperative detail will wreck.
igbo: Ị nọdị ala na-agụ ngwere ma ọdụ ekweghi ya

meaning: Troubles do not come singly: you are already in the water, and now soap has got into your eye.
equivalent: It never rains but it pours.
literal: You are in water, and soap has entered your eye.
usage: Said in sympathy when a person's troubles have piled one on top of another.
igbo: Ị nọ na mmiri, ncha abaa gị anya

meaning: People take the errand that carries a reward and refuse the one that is only sweat — service follows what is in it for the servant.
literal: If you send me an errand, send me to the rich man's; I will deliver it, but if you say run and bring it, I will not agree.
usage: Said of a person who chooses which errands to accept, taking the ones that pay and balking at the ones that only cost sweat.
igbo: I zie m ozi zie ogaranya, aga m ezi ya, mana ị sị gbaa ajụ bute ya, agaghị m ekwe

meaning: A load carried by two sits easy on the one in front and presses on the one behind — shared work is rarely shared evenly.
literal: The load that two people carry — it looks good to the person in front; it does not look good to the one carrying at the back.
usage: Said when the one who leads or stands in front takes the credit while the one behind carries the weight.
igbo: Ibu a dị mmadụ abụọ buru, ọ dịrị onye ihu mma ọ naghị adịrị onye bu n'azụ

meaning: What you don't know can't hurt you.
equivalent: What you don't know can't hurt you.
literal: The thing a person does not know does not kill him.
usage: Said to comfort someone who missed a danger or erred unknowingly.
igbo: Ihe onye na-amaghi anaghị egbu ya

meaning: A person's deeds are what bring them public notice, for good or ill.
equivalent: As you sow, so shall you reap.
literal: The thing a person does makes the bell call him.
usage: A warning that actions determine reputation and consequences.
igbo: Ihe onye na-eme ka ekwe na-akpọ ya

meaning: The same misfortune or misdeed weighs heavier on a great person than on a small one.
equivalent: The bigger they are, the harder they fall.
literal: The diarrhea that washes a cow is not like that of a goat.
usage: Used to remind a prominent person that their errors have larger consequences.
igbo: Ihe ọsọrọ afọ saa ehi, ọ gaghị aha ka ewu

meaning: [uncertain] One who has been hurt may turn and hurt others; the abused can become abusive.
literal: The thing that bit the dog is chewing a bad body.
usage: A warning against passing on one's pain to others.
igbo: Ihe tagburu nkịta na-ata ajọ arụ

meaning: An agreement offered by one who intends to devour you is no agreement at all.
literal: The thing the vulture agreed with the corpse.
usage: A warning not to trust a predator's promises.
igbo: Ihe udele kwere ozu

meaning: A face one knows is a beautiful face; familiarity makes a person dear.
literal: A known face is shining beauty.
usage: Said affectionately of a familiar or well-known person.
igbo: Ihu ama ama na-anyụ mma

meaning: Beauty does not help with hard work; good looks are no substitute for ability.
equivalent: Fine feathers do not make fine birds.
literal: A beautiful face is not good for making effort.
usage: A mild rebuke to someone relying on charm instead of effort.
igbo: Ihu dị mma adịghị mma ịtụ mbọ

meaning: Bravery and strength give a person a radiant, noble face.
literal: The face of a hero is shining beauty.
usage: Praise for a brave person whose courage makes them admirable.
igbo: Ihu dike na-anyụ mma

meaning: [uncertain] When a journey is pleasant, even the smallest creatures seem to sing its praise; success draws praise from all sides.
equivalent: Success has many fathers.
literal: A journey is beautiful, one travels it, worms are singing.
usage: Said when a good outcome brings unexpected praise or attention.
igbo: Ije maa mma e jee ya nje naabụ

meaning: A situation where either choice brings harm; you are caught between two evils.
equivalent: Damned if you do, damned if you don't.
literal: A fly perches on the breast/udder: if you leave it, it chews the breast/udder; if you strike it, you smash the seeds of the breast.
usage: Said when every available action carries a cost.
igbo: Ijiji berenyere na akpa amụ, ị hapụ ya ọ na-ata akpa amụ, ị kụa ya, ị kụpịa mkpụrụ amụ

meaning: Without good counsel, one follows bad company to ruin.
literal: A fly that has no adviser follows a corpse into the grave.
usage: A warning to seek counsel and avoid destructive company.
igbo: Ijiji na-enweghị onye ndụmọdụ na-eso ozu aba n’ili

meaning: Without good counsel, one follows bad company to ruin.
literal: A fly that has no adviser follows a corpse into the grave.
usage: A warning to seek counsel and avoid destructive company.
igbo: Ijiji enweghị onye ndụmọdụ na-eso ozu aba n’ili

meaning: [uncertain] When an elder's strength fails, the young people should give him honor and support.
literal: Strength has finished the old person; the young ones have become his honor.
usage: A call to respect and care for the aged in their weakness.
igbo: Ike gwụ agadị, ndịda abụrụ ya ugwu

meaning: A child may be too weak for work but strong for fighting or play; people find energy for what they like.
literal: Strength for work has finished the child; strength for fight is better than it.
usage: A rebuke to a child who is lazy at chores but eager for play.
igbo: Ike ọrụ gwụ nwata, ike ọgụ kara ya mma

meaning: He has reached his limit; his patience or endurance is exhausted.
equivalent: His cup is full.
literal: His cup has filled.
usage: Said when someone can take no more and is about to act.
igbo: Iko ya ejugo

meaning: [uncertain] Better to go hungry than to eat your fill and collapse on the road — stuffing yourself carries its own punishment.
literal: Rather than eat to fullness and fall on the road, one says one is fasting.
usage: Said to curb greed at a feast or in a season of plenty, when someone is piling food onto a plate as if there were no tomorrow.
igbo: Kama rijuo afọ dachie ụzọ sị buru ọnụ

meaning: [uncertain] Where is so-and-so when the trouble is biting? — the person who should help is nowhere to be found when the need is real.
literal: Where is egberigbe ọnụ when water is smarting the teeth?
usage: Thrown after someone who disappears when there is work or danger, or asked ruefully about the help that never came.
igbo: Kedụ ebe egberigbe ọnụ nọ mmiri na-ama eze

meaning: Some things happen in ways nobody can explain; you can only stand there and ask how.
literal: How does water enter into the horn of the ụgbọgụrụ?
usage: Said when something baffling or seemingly impossible has happened and no one can account for it.
igbo: Kedụ ka mmiri si banye n'opi ụgbọgụrụ?

meaning: An unripe pawpaw that has only tasted water is good for nothing — of what use is a thing that does not do what it exists to do?
literal: What use is the pawpaw that licked water?
usage: Said in dismissal of a person or thing that raises hopes and then delivers nothing.
igbo: Kedụ uru awayị tara mmiri?

meaning: [uncertain] The same hen's egg that becomes meat can also become fire — how does one thing turn into two such different things?
literal: And how does a hen's egg become meat, the one that it then becomes fire?
usage: Posed as a riddle or a wondering remark about something that turns out to have a second, surprising nature.
igbo: Kedụzi ka akwa ọkụkọ si bụrụ anụ, nke ọgazi abụrụ ọ́kụ̀?

meaning: [uncertain] However long you weave and weave it, once its head is cut off it turns into oshi — the same labour can end in something quite other than what was intended.
literal: Weave akwụ, weave akwụ; when its head is carried off, it becomes oshi.
usage: Said when a long effort comes to an unexpected or lesser end.
igbo: Kpara akwụ kpara akwụ, e buru isi ya, ọ bụrụ oshi

meaning: [uncertain] Get up and answer — this house is a place of pursuit, where everyone must be ready to respond.
literal: Stand up so that I may answer; the house is a search.
usage: Called out to rouse someone to stand up for the household when trouble is afoot.
igbo: Kulie ka m zaa ụlọ bụ ọchụchụ

meaning: A stitch in time saves nine.
equivalent: A stitch in time saves nine.
literal: Scoop out the water at the knee before it reaches the arm's shoulder.
usage: Said to urge someone, often a younger person, to correct a small fault before it grows beyond control.
igbo: Kupu mmiri nọ n'ikpere tupu o rue ubu aka

meaning: Nip it in the bud.
equivalent: Nip it in the bud.
literal: Bail the water while it is still in the mgbụgba ọla.
usage: Said to press someone to act on a problem now, while it is still small.
igbo: Kwọọ mmiri mgbe ọ ka dị na mgbụgba ọla

meaning: Telling your troubles to a rival wins you no pity — she answered my sickness with a dare to wrestle.
literal: I told my husband's wife that my stomach was troubling me; she told me to come out and wrestle.
usage: Said about a rival or hard-hearted neighbour who meets a complaint with a challenge instead of sympathy.
igbo: M gwara nwunye di m na afọ na-asa m, ọ sị m pụta mgba

meaning: [uncertain] What I feel for him is in the heart; what he feels for me is only in the eye — feeling given is not feeling returned.
literal: I am for him in the heart; he is for me in the eye.
usage: Said about a one-sided affection or a friendship in which only one side is sincere.
igbo: M taa na-abụ ya n'obi, ọ taa na-abụ m n'anya

meaning: [uncertain] Because there was also ama ama, Onitsha spoke to Obosi — a linked saying between neighbouring towns whose point cannot be recovered from this text.
literal: For the sake of adịkwa ama ama, Onitsha told Obosi.
usage: Kept as a chained saying between two neighbouring towns; as it stands here the line is too corrupt to pin to a situation.
igbo: Maka adịkwa ama ama Onịcha gwara Obosi

meaning: Strangers do not know who is who — away from your own place, nobody knows your standing.
literal: The people do not know the great one.
usage: Said to comfort someone whose worth goes unrecognised away from home, or to remark that standing is local.
igbo: Mba amaghị onye ukwu

meaning: [uncertain] Mbajị always outdoes what is seen in the fire — the point of the comparison is not recoverable from this line.
literal: Mbajị usually exceeds seeing in the fire.
usage: Used, as far as can be told, when something unforeseen outdoes what was plainly in view.
igbo: Mbajị na-akarị ịhụ n'ọkụ

meaning: Even the tortoise, the trickster of the tales, has no cunning in proverbs — nobody is clever in every arena.
literal: The tortoise is not crafty in proverb.
usage: Said of someone who is sharp in everything except the one place where sharpness is needed.
igbo: Mbe adịghị akọ n'ilu
Iwe dị n'obi, ọchị dị n'eze
meaning: A person can carry anger inside and still smile at you; a friendly face is not proof of a friendly heart.
literal: Anger is in the belly, laughter is in the teeth.
usage: Said to warn someone not to trust a smiling face, or to point out a person nursing a grudge behind polite talk.

igbo: Iwe nwanne anaghị eru n'okpụkpụ
meaning: Anger between siblings never goes so deep as to destroy them; quarrels inside a family pass without killing anyone.
literal: A sibling's anger does not reach the skull.
usage: Used to calm a quarrel between relatives, reminding them that kin remain kin when the anger cools.

igbo: Izu ka mma na nne ji
meaning: [uncertain] Taken as recorded ('izu is better with the mother yam'), the point cannot be recovered with confidence; it may be a damaged form of a proverb about yams and planting.
literal: Izu is better with the mother yam.
usage: Not safe to use as recorded; a speaker would need the fuller proverb before applying it.

igbo: Jiri anya okenye ji ele ihe dị n'ime akpa lee ya
meaning: Examine the matter the way an elder examines what is inside a bag: quietly, patiently, with long experience behind the looking.
literal: Use the eye an elder uses to look at what is inside a bag and look at it.
usage: Said when pushing someone to inspect a matter closely instead of rushing to a conclusion.

igbo: Jiri ehihie chọwa ewu ojii
meaning: Do a thing while the conditions for it still hold; act while it is still day.
equivalent: Make hay while the sun shines.
literal: Use the daytime to look for a black goat.
usage: Said to hurry someone along who is putting off a task until it can no longer be done.

igbo: Jiri ire gi gụọ eze gi ọnụ
meaning: Use your own tongue to count your own teeth: see to your own concerns before prying into anyone else's.
equivalent: Mind your own business.
literal: Use your tongue to count your teeth in your mouth.
usage: A mild rebuke to someone meddling in another person's affairs or talking too freely about them.

igbo: Jiri nwayọ ka ofe rọọrọ arọ zuoro gi nri
meaning: [uncertain] Go gently with it so that the soup, being mild, may feed you; patience is what lets a thing do you good.
literal: Use gentleness so that the soup being mild may feed you the food.
usage: Said to counsel patience when someone is rushing a task or bolting food too fast.

igbo: Ka a bịa ka a bịa, mere awọ epughi ọdụ
meaning: Let the thing be settled once and for all; the frog has no tail, and repeating the matter will not give it one.
literal: As one comes, so one comes, which is why the frog has no tail.
usage: Used to close a discussion that keeps going round in circles, or to state a plain fact that arguing cannot change.

igbo: Ka a na-aga n’ubi ka ọka na-aka
meaning: Keep going to the farm and the corn keeps ripening as you go; progress comes to the one who stays at the work.
literal: While one is going to the farm, the corn is ripening.
usage: Said to encourage someone to keep at a slow task instead of abandoning it for want of quick results.

igbo: Ka a na-achụ aja ka ikpe na-ama ndị mmụọ
meaning: [uncertain] The case against the spirits is being judged at the very hour the sacrifice is offered; matters move while the ritual is still going on.
literal: While they are offering sacrifice is while the case is judging the spirits.
usage: Said when events are moving faster than the discussion or ritual meant to settle them.

igbo: Ka a sị akụla ọgwụ ọ bụ ma ajụ?
meaning: [uncertain] If a person is warned off the medicine and leaves it alone, is that refusing it? — obeying a warning is not the same as rejecting what was offered.
literal: When one says do not take the medicine, is it that he refused?
usage: Said when a warning is mistaken for an argument, or when someone's compliance is read as defiance.

igbo: Ka aha eri, anaghị eri onwe ha
meaning: [uncertain] A name may be 'eaten' — maligned — but people do not eat one another; words do not consume the person they are aimed at.
literal: Even if a name is eaten, they do not eat one another.
usage: Said to console someone whose name is being spoken against, or to show the limits of talk.

igbo: Ka ahụtachaa ka mgbọ ji atụ enwe n'isi
meaning: It is only after looking well that the shot finds the monkey's head; consider before you act.
equivalent: Look before you leap.
literal: It is after one has seen clearly that the bullet hits the monkey on the head.
usage: Used to praise or demand careful thought before a decisive move.

igbo: Ka anyị kọọ n'ubi onye anyị bịara
meaning: A guest should plant something in the farm of the one who received him; hospitality is repaid by contributing, not by taking only.
literal: Let us plant in the farm of the person we came to.
usage: Said to urge a visitor or newcomer to leave something good behind among those who took him in.

igbo: Ka anyị na-achụ aja ka ikpe na-ama ndị mụọ
meaning: [uncertain] This is a variant of the preceding proverb: the case against the spirits is being judged while we are still offering sacrifice — the matter is being decided even as we act.
literal: While we are offering sacrifice is while the case is judging the spirits.
usage: Said when the outcome is being settled faster than the ritual or debate meant to influence it.

meaning: [uncertain] One who has lain long in trouble meets rescue with desperate haste — help that comes at last must not come slowly.
literal: The tortoise fell into a pit, stayed three nights; it reached the fourth night; it said to those who came to take it out: do it quickly, for the muck has already covered it.
usage: Said about someone who endured a bad situation a long time and then, when help finally arrives, is frantic for it to happen at once.
igbo: Mbe danyere n'olulu, nọọ abalị atọ, o ruo n'abali nke anọ, ọ sị ndị bịara iweputa ya, meeya ọsịịsọ na nshị eshigbuela ya

meaning: When disaster breaks out, the swift trample and escape, and it is the one who cannot run who is seized and blamed.
literal: The tortoise said that if war falls and tramples a pregnant woman, if war falls and those who have legs trample a pregnant woman, then they come and carry off the tortoise.
usage: Used when the slow or weak are made to answer for damage caused by those who were better able to get away.
igbo: Mbe sị na agha daa ọ zọgbuo nwaanyị dị ime, aghaa daa ndị nwere ụkwụ azọgbuo nwaanyị dị ime, abịa kpụrụ mbe

meaning: [uncertain] Grand duties are laid down for another man's affairs, but when the expense falls on the speaker he says he has nothing to bring.
literal: The tortoise said that one does not use a cow to bury his father who is near, but when he was told to bring it, he said he did not have it.
usage: Said to rebuke someone who prescribes lavish gestures with other people's property while contributing nothing himself.
igbo: Mbe sị na ejighi ehi kwaa nna ya dị na nso, mana a sị ya weta na ya enweghị

meaning: [uncertain] What a person cannot gather for himself is gathered for him by those around him — no one is left without help.
literal: The tortoise said: the one who did not gather, his ọgọdọ gathered for him.
usage: Said when family or neighbours cover for someone who could not gather his own share.
igbo: Mbe sị onye ekotaghị, ọgọdọ ya ekotara ya

meaning: [uncertain] Sleeping on a thing is not doing it; a man may dream of a whole meal and wake still hungry.
literal: The tortoise said: the one who sleeps and puts a spoon in his bag does not know the food that was eaten in a dream.
usage: Said to rouse someone who plans and wishes in his sleep but does nothing by day.
igbo: Mbe sị onye rahụwa ụra ya tinye ngajị n'akpa adịghị ama ama nri gbaa na nrọ

meaning: One person's downfall is another person's profit.
equivalent: It's an ill wind that blows nobody any good.
literal: The mgbada fell into the snare; it is the hunter's gain.
usage: Said when someone's misfortune turns into another person's opportunity.
igbo: Mgbada dara ibi, bụ uru dinta

meaning: Better to run for your life than to end up in the cooking pot — escape beats being caught.
literal: The mgbada said: rather than its head boiling in the pot, let swiftness be agreed to it.
usage: Said when someone chooses to slip away from danger instead of staying to be destroyed.
igbo: Mgbada sị kama isi ya ga agbọ n'ite, ka ikwukwe ọsọ kwee ya

meaning: [uncertain] A truncated line: it appears to say the tortoise has gone back into the ukpo bag; no settled teaching can be recovered from it.
literal: When the tortoise returned into the belly of the ukpo.
usage: A fragmentary line with no settled occasion for its use.
igbo: Mgbe mbe lọrọ afọ ukpo

meaning: What you do for another person you are doing for yourself.
literal: When a person has supported a person, it is as he supported himself.
usage: Said to encourage someone to help another, or to point out that kindness comes back to the giver.
igbo: Mgbe mmadụ kwara mmadụ ka ọ kwara onwe ya

meaning: [uncertain] Feeling ache or itch is the proof of life — a thing is known to be alive while it still hurts.
literal: When it is itching is when it is living.
usage: Said to console someone in pain, since suffering shows the sufferer is still alive.
igbo: Mgbe ọ na-ara ahụ ka ọ na-ebi

meaning: There is no fixed hour that makes it morning: a person's morning is whenever he wakes, so his day begins when he begins.
literal: When a person wakes from sleep is his morning.
usage: Said to reassure someone who is starting late that his own day has only just begun.
igbo: Mgbe onye jiri teta ụra bụ ụtụtụ ya

meaning: [uncertain] When what is needed is scarce, a person turns to his neighbour's hand — want makes people lean on one another.
literal: It is scarcity of leaves that makes the dibia use his fellow's hand.
usage: Said when someone who normally manages alone has to ask another for help.
igbo: Mkpa akwụkwọ ka dibịa ji aka ibe ya

meaning: Travel is a good thing: it was on the road that the he-goat learned to hold his head high — the road teaches what home cannot.
equivalent: Travel broadens the mind.
literal: The he-goat said that travelling in other lands is good, that it was on its journey that it learned to raise its muzzle up.
usage: Said to praise travelling and the experience and bearing it gives a person.
igbo: Mkpi si na ije mba amaka, na ọ bụ na njem ya ka ya mụtụra ibili ọnụ elu

meaning: [uncertain] The he-goat put out horns because its mother had horns; the ram's own case came out otherwise — a child's conduct is credited to the parent, though each one's own outcome differs.
literal: The he-goat grew horns because its mother grew horns; the ram did its own differently.
usage: Said when someone's behaviour is traced to their parents, or when the same upbringing yields a different result.
igbo: Mkpi puru mpi maka na nne ya puru mpi, ebula mere nke ya nsata

meaning: [uncertain] The he-goat grew horns because its mother had horns, while the ram came by its own by its own doing — the same result may be inherited or earned.
literal: The he-goat grew horns because its mother grew horns; the ram drank its own portion.
usage: Said when comparing what a person owes to inheritance with what he has made for himself.
igbo: Mkpi puru mpi maka na nne ya puru mpi, ebula ṅutara nke ya aṅuta

meaning: When a sacred or great presence departs, it is handled with both hands; important departures deserve care and respect.
literal: As the deity is leaving, one uses two hands to carry it.
usage: Used to urge that a great person or sacred thing be given a careful, respectful send-off.
igbo: Ka arụsị na-ahana, e ji aka abụọ apa ya

meaning: [uncertain] Only after careful examination can one see exactly how something happened.
literal: When one has looked carefully, how the bullet uses to shoot the monkey in the head.
usage: Used to urge patience and close attention before drawing conclusions.
igbo: Ka e letachaa ka mgbọ ji atụ enwe n'isi

meaning: If the calf is the one used to test the knife, its mother should not be killed for it; do not punish kin for one person's deed.
literal: If a calf was used to test the knife, should one say its mother be killed?
usage: Used to object to collective punishment or blaming a family for one member's action.
igbo: Ka ejiri nwa ehi mma atụ, asị gbuo nne ya?

meaning: [uncertain] Every creature carries a load suited to its own size; each has its own burden and capacity.
literal: As the elephant's head is to its body, so is the ant's also.
usage: Used to acknowledge that people's burdens and abilities differ.
igbo: Ka ishi enyi si anyị ya arụ, ka nke ndanda si anyị kwa ya

meaning: Do not blame me for a natural state of affairs; my arrival did not cause the lizard to be hairless.
literal: Let me come, let me come, made the lizard not grow hair.
usage: Used to reject an absurd or unfair accusation.
igbo: Ka m bịa ka m bia mere ngwere agbaghị ajị

meaning: [uncertain] A child can die while doing something as ordinary as basking in the sun; tragedy can strike without warning.
literal: When I return, my child who came to bask in the sun has died.
usage: Used to express the shock of an unexpected death in ordinary circumstances.
igbo: Ka m lawa na nwa m bịara iku anwụọla

meaning: [uncertain] If I put you behind me or rely on you, I still end up doing the work myself.
equivalent: If you want something done right, do it yourself.
literal: If I put you at the back, I cook work.
usage: Used to complain that a helper is useless and the speaker must do the task alone.
igbo: Ka m tunye gị azụ, esi m oru

meaning: [uncertain] A knife is as its sheath is made; the outer covering tells you about the thing it holds.
literal: As the knife is, so is how its sheath is sewn.
usage: Used to remark that presentation or covering reflects the quality of what is inside.
igbo: Ka mma dị ka esi akwa ọbọ ya

meaning: [uncertain] When you start a task, finish it thoroughly—clean the leg and clean the tongue too.
literal: As one washes the leg, so one washes its tongue.
usage: Used to urge thoroughness and completing a task.
igbo: Ka na-ahọ ụkwa ka ana-ahọ ire ya

meaning: A person is reflected in the community or faith they belong to.
equivalent: A man is known by the company he keeps.
literal: As a person is, so is his church.
usage: Used to say that people's associations reveal their character.
igbo: Ka onye dị ka ụka ya dị

meaning: If Okeke has gone to the army, where are his boots? Claims mean nothing without the evidence that goes with them.
equivalent: The proof of the pudding is in the eating.
literal: After Okeke went to the army, where are his boots?
usage: Used to challenge someone who boasts of an achievement but shows no sign of it.
igbo: Ka Okeke gachara army , olee boot ya?

meaning: The same situation applies everywhere; what is so in one place is so in another.
literal: As it is at the rat's place, so it is at the lizard's place.
usage: Used to say that a condition is universal or that no one is exempt.
igbo: Ka ọ dị be oke, ka ọ dị be ngwere

meaning: [uncertain] Rather than let an animal struggle with me, I cut off its tail; I reduce an opponent's strength before facing them.
literal: Rather than the animal that will struggle with me, I cut its tail.
usage: Used to explain a preemptive move that weakens a future opponent.
igbo: Kama anụ m ga-agbalarị m, m bere ya ọdụ

meaning: If the water is going to swallow me, let it serve as my hat; prepare for inevitable trouble and turn it to your advantage.
equivalent: Forewarned is forearmed.
literal: Rather than water swallowing me, let it be my cap.
usage: Used to urge preparation for an unavoidable difficulty.
igbo: Kama mmiri ga-erim, ya buru okpu m

meaning: If the dibia's own child must die, then every medicinal root in the bush is exhausted; even the most skilled cannot always save their own.
literal: Rather than the dibia's child dying, let the roots finish in the bush.
usage: Used when someone's expertise fails to solve a problem close to home.
igbo: Kama nnwa dibịa ga-anwụ, ka mgbọrọgwụ gwụ n'ọhịa

meaning: Water is what turns soap into foam: nothing gets done by one thing alone, and the helper deserves as much credit as the effort.
literal: Water is helping soap to foam.
usage: Said to invite someone to lend a hand, or to praise the quiet helper without whom the work would never have come out.
igbo: Mmiri na-enyere ncha aka agba ụfụfụ

meaning: [uncertain] If the water has swallowed the elephant, the tortoise plucking its leaves is left asking whether it will fly or whether it will sink — when the strong go under, the weak can only wonder how they will escape.
literal: Water swallowed elephant, as tortoise saw and was breaking off ọgọdọ, will it fly or will it swim?
usage: Used as a warning when the fall of someone great shows that no one is safe.
igbo: Mmiri riri enyi ka mbe huru na awa ọgọdọ, ọ ga-efe efe ka ọ ga-awụ awụ?

meaning: The same source serves everyone: the great take what they need from it in their own measure, and so do the small.
literal: The water the eagle used to wash its hands is the water the ugbala used to wash its body.
usage: Said to settle a quarrel over who deserves more, reminding the parties that one shared thing feeds all of them.
igbo: Mmiri ugo jiri kwọọ aka ka ugbala jiri saa ahụ

meaning: Whoever lends you the power to do a thing is expected to help you carry what comes of it; help that stops halfway is no help.
literal: The spirit that led the child, if it killed an ele, will it help it or will it carry it for it?
usage: A rebuke to an elder or patron who set someone on a task and then walked away from the consequences.
igbo: Mmụọ kpara nwata ọ gbagbuo ele, ga enyere ya aka ọ maburu ya

meaning: People are destroyed by the very things they give themselves to; the spirits a person serves are the ones that kill him.
literal: The spirits they are worshipping are killing them.
usage: Said with a shake of the head about someone whose chosen attachments are ruining him.
igbo: Mmụọ ndị na-efe na-egbu ha

meaning: [uncertain] What a person leaves behind after eating shows who he is — the remains on the dish betray the one who eats beyond his share.
literal: It is by the leftovers on the ụkwa that one knows the person of much food.
usage: A dry remark about a greedy eater or a covetous person whose behaviour gives him away.
igbo: Na ntụtụ ụkwa ka e ji ama onye ụbụ nri

meaning: Growth comes with the years; a child washes and grows one year at a time, and nothing worthwhile arrives all at once.
literal: It is year by year that a child washes its body.
usage: A consolation to someone impatient for a child, a harvest, or a slow improvement to arrive.
igbo: N'afọ n'afọ ka nwata na-asa ahụ

meaning: Patience is the road the world is travelled on; the one who can wait is the one who goes far.
literal: Patience is the journey of the world.
usage: Said to steady a person who is in a hurry and tempted to force a matter open.
igbo: Ndidi bu ije ụwa

meaning: Each lives by the other — the water is the fish's life, and the fish is the water's life; no one thrives apart from what sustains him.
literal: Life of water, life of fish.
usage: Said of two people or peoples so bound together that harm to one is harm to the other.
igbo: Ndụ mmiri, ndụ azụ

meaning: Nothing sells itself at home; you must get up and move about if you want the goat sold.
literal: It is by going about that one sells a young goat.
usage: An encouragement to a trader or a job-seeker to stop sitting still and take the matter out into the world.
igbo: Ngagharị ka e ji ere nwa mkpi

meaning: [uncertain] Showing up where people gather is what brings a full belly home — you are fed by attending, not by staying away.
literal: Gathering a meeting brings a belly of rice.
usage: Said lightly to urge someone to come along to a gathering rather than keep to himself.
igbo: Ngakọ meeting na-ebuta ụbụ rice

meaning: [uncertain] What has been covered over is uncovered again once there is need of it — nothing set aside is lost for good.
literal: Ngala covered the mat; when it is wanted, it is uncovered.
usage: A consolation to someone who has put a thing away or been put aside, promising it can still be brought out.
igbo: Ngala kpuchie ute, agụọ ekpughee ya

meaning: An elder runs after the straying cow, but he runs with dignity — even a needed, unseemly act is done with self-respect intact.
literal: It is with pride that an elder runs after a cow.
usage: Said to defend or to tease an elder who has been seen doing something beneath his station for gain.
igbo: Nganga ka okenye ji agbara ehi ọsọ

meaning: Abandon the place that shelters you and you are caught in the open; leaving your cover is how you are taken.
literal: The lizard left the base of the tree; the hand caught it.
usage: A warning to someone restless to leave a safe position for no good reason.
igbo: Ngwere hapụ ukwu osisi, aka akpara ya

meaning: Lizards all lie flat the same way, so no one can tell whose belly is aching — outward likeness hides what each person is carrying inside.
literal: All lizards lie flat the same; we do not know the one the belly is hurting.
usage: Said to soften someone's judgment of others, or to explain why a person who looks fine may be suffering.
igbo: Ngwere niile makpu amakpu anyị amaghị nke afọ na-arụ

meaning: Outward achievements or associations do not change what a person fundamentally is.
literal: The lizard that climbed the kola nut is not a child.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who thinks a feat or a new association has made them something they are not.
igbo: Ngwere rịrị ọjị abụzighi nwa

meaning: [uncertain] When you set out on your own and fall, you have no one to blame but yourself, since you were your own trainer.
literal: The lizard said that it falls from the top, says there is no one who raised it, let it raise its own self.
usage: Used as a rebuke to someone who wants to blame others after a self-chosen risk goes wrong.
igbo: Ngwere sị na-elu daa, si enweghi onye toro ya, ya too onye ya

meaning: A matter that can be unravelled patiently should not be forced open; rough handling creates a debt you must answer for.
literal: A bundle that will be untied piece by piece, splitting it with the hand is answering for it.
usage: Used as a warning to handle a delicate matter patiently rather than with force.
igbo: Ngwugwu a ga-atọpe atọpe, ịwa ya aka bụ ịza

meaning: You can run, but you can't hide.
equivalent: You can run, but you can't hide.
literal: The nkakwu bird hides so that the vulture will not carry it; the vulture said it is carrying the nkakwu.
usage: Used to say that a person cannot escape a pursuer or fate by hiding.
igbo: Nkakwụ na-ezo ka udele ghara ibu ya, udele o kwuru na ya na-ebu nkakwụ

meaning: [uncertain] What a person has is what he holds in his hand; people can only rely on what is truly theirs.
literal: What a person holds is how he holds in hand.
usage: Used to say that each person must depend on what is actually in their own possession.
igbo: Nke onye ji ka o ji ana aka

meaning: As you sow, so shall you reap.
equivalent: As you sow, so shall you reap.
literal: What a person ate is what he carries.
usage: Used to remind someone that they must bear the consequences of their own actions.
igbo: Nke onye riri ka o bu

meaning: If you chase two rabbits, you will catch neither.
equivalent: If you chase two rabbits, you will catch neither.
literal: A dog answers two calls at one time and also breaks a calabash.
usage: Used as a warning against divided attention or trying to satisfy two demands at once.
igbo: Nkịta na-aza oku abụo ofu mgbe, na-etiwakwa agba
